[p. 281] It does not conflict with the verses of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*), because they abrogate it (*nasikhah*, through *naskh*, abrogation).

**قَوْلُهُ تَعالى:** ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلَنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا شَياطِينَ الإنْسِ والجِنِّ﴾ **الآيَةَ** ("His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾, the verse.")

ذَكَرَ تَعالى في (p-491) هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ أنَّهُ جَعَلَ لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا، وبَيَّنَ هُنا أنَّ أعْداءَ الأنْبِياءِ هم شَياطِينُ الإنْسِ والجِنِّ، وصَرَّحَ في مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ أنَّ أعْداءَ الأنْبِياءِ مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ، وهو قَوْلُهُ: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْنا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ [الفرقان: ٣١]؛ فَدَلَّ ذَلِكَ عَلى أنَّ المُرادَ بِالمُجْرِمِينَ شَياطِينُ الإنْسِ والجِنِّ.

(Exalted is He) mentioned in this noble verse that He appointed an enemy for every prophet, and He explained here that the enemies of the prophets are the devils of mankind and jinn. In another place He stated explicitly that the enemies of the prophets are among the criminals, namely His saying: ﴿And thus We appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan: 31]. This indicates that what is meant by "the criminals" is the devils of mankind and jinn.

وذَكَرَ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ أنَّ مِنَ الإنْسِ شَياطِينَ، وصَرَّحَ بِذَلِكَ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿وَإذا خَلَوْا إلى شَياطِينِهِمْ قالُوا إنّا مَعَكُمْ﴾ الآيَةَ [البقرة: ١٤]، وقَدْ جاءَ الخَبَرُ بِذَلِكَ مَرْفُوعًا مِن حَدِيثِ أبِي ذَرٍّ عِنْدَ الإمامِ أحْمَدَ وغَيْرِهِ.

He mentioned in this verse that there are devils among mankind, and He stated this explicitly in His saying: ﴿And when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], **the verse**. And the report to this effect has come as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) hadith from the narration of Abu Dharr, in (the Musnad of) Imam Ahmad and others.

والعَرَبُ تُسَمِّي كُلَّ مُتَمَرِّدٍ شَيْطانًا، سَواءٌ كانَ مِنَ الجِنِّ أوْ مِنَ الإنْسِ كَما ذَكَرْنا، أوْ مِن غَيْرِهِما، وفي الحَدِيثِ: «الكَلْبُ الأسْوَدُ شَيْطانٌ».

The Arabs call every rebellious (transgressor) a shaytan, whether he is from the jinn or from mankind as we have mentioned, or from other than them. And in the hadith: "The black dog is a shaytan."

وقَوْلُهُ: شَياطِينُ، بَدَلٌ (substitute, i.e., apposition) مِن قَوْلِهِ: عَدُوًّا، أوْ مَفْعُولٌ أوَّلُ لِـ ”جَعَلْنا“، والثّانِي: ”عَدُوًّا“، أيْ: جَعَلْنا شَياطِينَ الإنْسِ والجِنِّ عَدُوًّا.

And His saying, شَياطِينَ (shayatin), is either a badal (apposition) of His saying عَدُوًّا (aduwwan), or the first object of جَعَلْنا (ja'alna), and the second is عَدُوًّا (aduwwan), meaning: We made the devils of mankind and jinn an enemy.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾. In this noble verse He mentions that obeying most of the people of the earth is misguidance. He makes clear in other passages that most of the people of the earth are not believers, and that this occurs among past nations,

• like His saying: ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾ [al-Ra'd: 1],

• and His saying: ﴿And most of mankind will not believe, even if you strive eagerly﴾ [Yusuf: 103],

• and His saying: ﴿And most of the earlier peoples had already gone astray before them﴾ [al-Saffat: 71],

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 8],

along with other verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 119:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾ — the verse. The verified view is that He detailed it for them by His saying: ﴿Say, "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion"﴾ — the verse [al-An'am: 145]. The meaning of the verse is: what prevents you from eating what you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum, i.e. ritually slaughtered) and over which you have mentioned the name of Allah? And the situation is that Allah has detailed for you what is forbidden for you to eat in His saying: ﴿Say, "I do not find in what has been revealed to me"﴾ — the verse [al-An'am: 145]. This is not from Him (i.e. it is not the detailing referred to).

As for what many of the exegetes (mufassirun, plural of mufassir, an interpreter of the Qur'an) claim, that He detailed it for them by His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion﴾ — the verse [al-Ma'idah: 3], this is an error; because His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Prohibited to you are carrion﴾ is from Surat al-Ma'idah, which is among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an in Madinah, whereas His saying: ﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾ [119] is from Surat al-An'am, which is Meccan. So the truth is what we have mentioned, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals to scheme therein﴾, the verse. In this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, mentions that He placed in every town its greatest criminals to scheme therein. He does not explain here who is meant by "the greatest" (akabir), nor the manner of their scheming. He explains all of that in other places. He explains that its greatest criminals are the people of affluence (al-taraf) and luxury in this world, in His saying: ﴿And We did not send a warner to any town but that its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent"﴾ [Saba': 34], and His saying: ﴿And likewise, We did not send before you a warner to any town but that its affluent ones said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]. And similar verses.

He also explains that the scheming of the greatest criminals mentioned is their ordering [people] to disbelieve in Allah, exalted is He, and to set up rivals to Him, in His saying: ﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Rather, [it was] the scheming of night and day when you were ordering us to disbelieve in Allah and to set up rivals to Him"﴾ [Saba': 33], and His saying: ﴿And they schemed a great scheme﴾ ﴿And they said, "Do not leave your gods"﴾, the verse [Nuh: 22, 23].

The two most apparent grammatical analyses (i'rab, the study of the grammatical function of words in a sentence) of the verse in my view are two:

The first: akabir (أكابرَ) is in construct with mujrimiha (مُجْرِمِيها, "its criminals"), and it is the first object of ja'ala (جَعَلَ), used here in the sense of sayyara (صَيَّرَ, "to make/render"). The second object is the prepositional phrase, namely "in every town" (في كُلِّ قَرْيَةٍ).

The second: mujrimiha (مُجْرِمِيها) is the first object, and akabir (أكابرَ) is the second object, meaning: "We made its criminals its greatest ones." Here akabir is the plural of akbar (الأكْبَرِ, "greatest").

Shinqiti's commentary (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 124:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When a sign comes to them, they say, "We will not believe until we are given the like of what the messengers of Allah were given."﴾ They mean that they will not believe until the angels bring them the message, as they brought it to the messengers, as He explained in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why were angels not sent down to us, or [why] do we not see our Lord?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], and His saying: ﴿Or you bring Allah and the angels before us as guarantors﴾ [al-Isra': 92], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 125:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾, and the rest of the verse.

It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about this noble verse, and it was said: "How is his breast expanded, O Messenger of Allah?" He (ﷺ) said: "It is a light that is cast into it, so it expands and widens." They said: "Is there a sign by which this can be recognized?" He said: "Turning in repentance to the abode of eternity (al-khuld), withdrawing from the abode of delusion (al-ghurur), and preparing for death before the encounter with death."

And his saying, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has expanded to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord...?﴾ [al-Zumar: 22].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 128:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will say: The Fire is your abode, wherein you shall abide forever, except as Allah wills﴾, and so on.

This noble verse implies that the punishment of the people of the Fire is not everlasting without any cessation, ever. A parallel to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is groaning and wailing﴾ ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 106-107], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Remaining therein for ages﴾ [An-Naba': 23].

Verses have also come indicating that their punishment has no cessation, such as His saying: ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ [An-Nisa': 57].

The answer to this is in several respects:

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿except as Allah wills﴾ means: except those whom Allah wills not to abide therein, from among the people of major sins among the monotheists.

It is established in the authentic hadiths that some of the people of the Fire will come out of it, and they are the people of major sins among the monotheists. Ibn Jarir transmitted this view from Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Sinan and Khalid ibn Ma'dan, and Ibn Jarir chose it. The scope of "ma" in this view is the use of "ma" to mean "man" (who). Its parallel in the Qur'an is: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [An-Nisa': 3].

The second: the period which Allah excepted is the period between their being raised from their graves and their settling in their final abode. This was also said by Ibn Jarir.

The third respect: His saying, ﴿except as Allah wills﴾, contains generality (ijmal), and the verses and authentic hadiths have come explicitly stating that they abide therein forever, and their apparent meaning is an everlasting abiding without cessation. Apparent meaning is among the factors of preference, so the apparent is given precedence over the general (mujmal), as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul).

And among them: that "illa" (except) in Surat Hud means "siwa" (other than): except what Allah wills of an addition to the duration of the heavens and the earth.

Some scholars said: the exception is on its apparent sense, and that there will come upon the Fire a time in which no one will be in it.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "There will certainly come upon Jahannam a time when its doors will swing, with no one in it, and that is after they have remained for ages."

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it will consume them by Allah's command.

The one who qualifies it, may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that this Fire in which no one will remain must be understood as the tier in which the disobedient Muslims were, as al-Baghawi affirmed in his tafsir, because by it the evidences are reconciled, and acting upon both evidences is better than disregarding one of them.

The scholars have agreed on the obligation of reconciliation when it is possible. As for what many scholars among the Companions and those after them say, that the Fire will perish and the punishment will cease for its people, the Qur'anic verses require that this be unsound. Its clarification: the situation cannot be free of one of five states by correct division, and anything else reverts to these.

The first: that it is said the Fire will perish, and their relief from punishment is due to its perishing.

The second: that it is said they died while it remains.

The third: that it is said they were brought out of it while it remains.

The fourth: that it is said they will remain in it, but the punishment will be lightened for them.

The removal of punishment entirely and its impossibility are not mentioned among the divisions, because we establish proof against the negation of the lightening of punishment, and negating its lightening entails negating its removal and its impossibility, so we are content with it, since its negation indicates the negation of both. All four of these divisions are shown by the Qur'an to be false.

As for its perishing, Allah has explicitly denied it by His saying: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [Al-Isra': 97].

Allah, exalted is He, has said, ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107], concerning the abiding of the people of Paradise and the abiding of the people of the Fire, and He clarified the absence of cessation in the abiding of the people of Paradise by His saying: ﴿a gift unbroken﴾ [Hud: 108], and by His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Sad: 54], and His saying: ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah remains﴾ [An-Nahl: 96].

He clarified the absence of cessation in the abiding of the people of the Fire by His saying: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾.

So whoever says that the Fire has a dying down after which there is no increase in blaze is refuted by this noble verse. It is known that "kullama" (every time) requires repetition with the repetition of the act that follows it. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We replace them with other skins﴾ [An-Nisa': 56].

As for their death, Allah has explicitly denied it by His saying: ﴿Nor will it be decreed for them so they would die﴾ [Fatir: 36];

• and His saying: ﴿Neither dying therein nor living﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74];

• and His saying: ﴿Death will come to him from every place, but he will not die﴾ [Ibrahim: 17].

The Prophet (ﷺ) clarified in an authentic hadith that death will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a white-horned ram, and it will be slaughtered, and when death is slaughtered, certainty is attained that there is no death, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It will be said: O people of Paradise, eternity, so there is no death; and O people of the Fire, eternity without death."

As for their being brought out of it, Allah has explicitly denied it by His saying: ﴿And they will not be removed from the Fire﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 167], and by His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, they will be returned into it﴾ [As-Sajdah: 20], and by His saying: ﴿And they will not come out of it, and for them is a lasting punishment﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 37].

As for the lightening of punishment for them, Allah has explicitly denied it by His saying: ﴿Its punishment will not be lightened for them. Thus We recompense every ungrateful one﴾ [Fatir: 36];

• and His saying: ﴿So We will not increase you except in punishment﴾ [An-Naba': 30];

• and His saying: ﴿It will not be relaxed for them, and they therein are despairing﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 75];

• and His saying: ﴿Indeed, its punishment was ever adhering﴾ [Al-Furqan: 65];

• and His saying: ﴿So it will be an inseparable punishment﴾ [Al-Furqan: 77];

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So their punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾ [An-Nahl: 85].

And His saying: ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 37]. It is not hidden that His saying, ﴿nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾, and His saying, ﴿It will not be relaxed for them﴾, are both verbs in a context of negation, so the negative particle negates the verbal noun (masdar) contained in the verb, meaning there is no lightening of punishment for them and no slackening of it. The claim that it perishes entails the lightening and slackening that are negated in these verses, rather it entails their removal entirely, just as it entails the negation of the constancy of the punishment that is stated by His saying: ﴿So it will be an inseparable punishment﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, its punishment was ever adhering﴾, and its permanence that is stated by His saying: ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾.

The apparent meaning of these verses is the non-perishing of the Fire, which is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾. As for what some scholars argued, that even if it were supposed that Allah informed of its non-perishing, that would not prevent its perishing, because it is a threat (wa'id), and breaking a threat is praiseworthy and not blameworthy, and that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He does not break His promise (wa'd) but did not mention that He does not break His threat (wa'id), and that the poet said:

"Even if I threaten him or promise him, I am one who breaks my threat, and fulfils my promise."

The apparent meaning is that this is unsound for two reasons:

The first: it entails that it is permissible for a disbeliever not to enter the Fire, because the report of that is a threat, and breaking it according to this view is not a problem.

The second: He, exalted is He, has explicitly stated the truth of His threat against those who denied His messengers, when He said: ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My threat was realized﴾ [Qaf: 14].

It has been established in the method of explicit text among the methods of causation (masalik al-'illah) that the fa' (then) is among the particles of causation, as in the saying: "He forgot, so he prostrated," meaning he prostrated because of his forgetfulness, and "He stole, so his hand was cut off," meaning because of his theft. So His saying: ﴿Each of them denied the messengers, so My threat was realized﴾ means the threat became due to be carried out against them because of their denial of the messengers. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There was not one but denied the messengers, so My punishment was due﴾ [Sad: 14].

Among the explicit proofs on this is His statement, exalted is He, that His word is not changed regarding what He threatened the people of the Fire with, when He said: ﴿Do not dispute before Me, for I had already presented to you the threat﴾ ﴿The word is not changed with Me, and I am not unjust to the servants﴾ [Qaf: 28-29].

For this there is supporting evidence in the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when no father will avail his son...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ [Luqman: 33], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is to occur﴾ [At-Tur: 7]. So the apparent meaning is that the threat which may be broken is the threat against disobedient believers, because Allah clarified that by His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa': 48].

Thus, when it becomes clear from these texts that all these divisions are false, the fifth division is determined, which is their abiding therein forever without cessation or lightening, by correct division and examination.

There is no strangeness in that, for their natural corruption is permanent and does not cease, so their recompense is permanent and does not cease.

The evidence that their corruption does not cease is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ [Al-Anfal: 23].

His saying "khayran" (any good) is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, so it is general. Had there been in them any good at any time, Allah would have known it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [Al-An'am: 28]. Their returning after witnessing the punishment is not strange; after it, their returning after direct experience of the punishment is no more strange, since seeing the punishment with one's own eyes is like falling into it, especially since Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, and today your sight is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22], and He said: ﴿How well they will hear and see on the Day they come to Us﴾ [Maryam: 38].

The punishment of the disbelievers is for humiliation and retribution, not for purification and expiation, as Allah, exalted is He, indicated by His saying: ﴿And He will not purify them﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 174], and by His saying: ﴿And for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178]. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

(p-٤٩٣) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ — the verse.

Some scholars said: By "messengers" from among the jinn is meant their warners, who listen to the words of the messengers and convey them to their people. What supports this is that God mentioned that they are warners to their people in His saying: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn, listening to the Qur'an; so when they attended it they said, "Be silent." Then when it was finished, they turned back to their people as warners﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29].

Some scholars said: ﴿messengers from among you﴾ [al-An'am: 130] means from your collective, specifically the humans, the truthful ones; for there are no messengers from the jinn. This view finds support in that the Qur'an sometimes uses the whole to refer to a part of it, like His saying: ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], and His saying: ﴿but they denied him and hamstrung her﴾ [al-Shams: 14], although the one who hamstrung her was only one of them, as He clarified with His saying: ﴿they called their companion, and he took it up and hamstrung﴾ [al-Qamar: 29].

Know that what al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) and others among the eminent scholars mentioned in interpreting this verse, namely that His saying: ﴿from which come forth pearls and coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22] refers only to the salt sea to the exclusion of the fresh water, is a grave error that cannot be upheld. It clearly contradicts the words of God Most High, for God mentioned the two seas, the salt and the fresh, in His saying: ﴿The two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and this one is salty and bitter﴾ [Fatir: 12]. He then explicitly stated the extraction of pearls and coral from both of them together in His saying: ﴿and from each you eat fresh meat and extract ornaments that you wear﴾. The ornament mentioned is pearls and coral, so restricting it to the salt sea clearly contradicts the verse, as you can see.

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people were heedless.﴾ The negation in this noble verse is directed at the circumstantial clause (al-jumlah al-haliyyah), and the meaning is that He does not destroy a people in a state of their heedlessness, that is, in a state of not having been warned. Rather, He does not destroy anyone except after proof has been established and warning has been given through the tongues of the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, as He explained this meaning in many verses:

• such as His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a Messenger﴾ [al-Isra' 17:15],

• and His saying: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good tidings and warners, so that mankind would have no argument against Allah after the Messengers﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:165],

• and His saying: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 35:24],

• and His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a Messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the Taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl 16:36],

and other verses to that effect."

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 1 of 6):**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾, etc.

The scholars differed over what is meant by this "due" mentioned here, and whether it has been abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e. superseded by a later ruling through *naskh*, abrogation) or not. A group of scholars said: this due is the obligatory *zakat* (the prescribed alms-tax). Among those who held this view were Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Abbas, Tawus, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and Malik. Al-Qurtubi transmitted this from them. Ibn Kathir transmitted it from Anas, Sa'id, and others, and Ibn Jarir transmitted it from Ibn Abbas, Anas, al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, Tawus, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd.

Another group said: it does not mean *zakat*. Rather, what is meant is that one gives to the needy who are present on the day of the harvest a handful, a bundle, and the like. Some of them took this to be obligatory and some took it to be recommended (*nadb*). Al-Qurtubi said: Ali ibn al-Husayn, Ata', al-Hakam, Hammad, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid said: it is a right in the wealth other than *zakat*, which God commanded as a recommendation. It is also reported from Ibn Umar and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ). Mujahid said: "When you reap and the needy come to you, throw to them some of the ears of grain. When you cut the palm-fronds, throw to them some of the palm-spathes. When you thresh and winnow it, throw some of it to them. When you know its measure, take out its *zakat* from it."

Another group said: it is an obligatory right other than *zakat*, and it is not fixed to a specific amount. Among those who held this was Ata', as Ibn Jarir transmitted from him.

Another group said: it has been abrogated by *zakat*. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and al-Shawkani attributed it in his *Tafsir* to the majority of scholars. He supported it by saying that this surah is Meccan, while the verse of *zakat* was revealed in Medina in the second year after the Hijrah.

Ibn Kathir said: "There is an issue with the claim of abrogation, because it was something obligatory originally, and then its explanation was detailed and its quantity and amount were specified." They said: "This was in the second year of the Hijrah. And God knows best." End of quotation from Ibn Kathir.

His meaning is that the legislation of *zakat* is an explanation of this due, not an abrogation of it. Among those who transmitted from them the view of abrogation were Ibn Abbas, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, Tawus, Abu al-Sha'tha', Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Juraij. Al-Shawkani transmitted this from them, and so did al-Qurtubi, and he also transmitted it from al-Suddi and Atiyyah. Ibn Jarir also transmitted it from Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Atiyyah. Ibn Jarir argued for abrogation by the consensus (*ijma'*) that the *zakat* on crops is not taken except after winnowing and cleaning, and the *zakat* on dates is not taken except after the dates are picked. This indicates that nothing is taken on the day of harvest. Thus it is known that the verse is abrogated, or that it is meant as a recommendation. The matter is clear.

And if what is meant by it is *zakat*, then it has been indicated that this mentioned due is the portion of wealth that is obligatory on the *nisab* (the minimum threshold) in the verses about *zakat*. This is what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:267], and the Sunnah has explained it. When you know this, know that three matters need to be clarified here:

The first: determining what *zakat* is obligatory on from what the earth produces.

The second: determining the amount on which *zakat* is obligatory.

The third: determining the amount that is obligatory, which we will explain in detail, God willing.

Know first that there is no disagreement among the scholars regarding the obligation of *zakat* on wheat, barley, dates, and raisins.

They differed regarding other things produced by the earth. A group said: there is no *zakat* on anything else of all that the earth produces. This was reported from al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and al-Sha'bi. Among the Kufans who held this were Ibn Abi Layla, al-Thawri, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ibn al-Mubarak, and Yahya ibn Adam, and Abu Ubayd went this way.

This was also reported from Abu Musa, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is the view of Abu Musa, for he would not take *zakat* except from wheat, barley, dates, and raisins. Waki' related this from Talhah ibn Yahya, from Abu Burdah, from his father, as al-Qurtubi transmitted from them.

The proponents of this view relied on what al-Daraqutni narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Amr, that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) only instituted *zakat* on wheat, barley, dates, and raisins." In another narration, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The tenth (*'ushr*) is on dates, raisins, wheat, and barley." And from Musa ibn Talhah, from Umar, that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) only instituted *zakat* on these four: wheat, barley, dates, and raisins." And from Abu Burdah, from Abu Musa and Mu'adh: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent them both to Yemen to teach the people the matters of their religion, and he commanded them not to take charity except from these four: wheat, barley, dates, and raisins." All of these were narrated by al-Daraqutni, as Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*.

The author of this commentary (may God pardon him) says: As for what al-Daraqutni narrated from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet (ﷺ) only instituted *zakat* on the four mentioned, its chain is weak, because it is from the narration of Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah al-Azrami, who is abandoned (*matruk*), as Ibn Hajar said in *al-Talkhis*. As for what al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of Musa ibn Talhah, from Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ) only instituted *zakat* on the four mentioned, Abu Zur'ah said about it: "Musa from Umar is *mursal* (a narration with a missing companion in the chain)," as Ibn Hajar also said. As for what he attributed to al-Daraqutni from Abu Burdah, from Abu Musa and Mu'adh, it was narrated by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi from Abu Burdah, from both of them.

Al-Bayhaqi said: "Its narrators are trustworthy (*thiqat*), and it is connected (*muttasil*)," as Ibn Hajar also said.

Malik and his companions said: *zakat* is obligatory on every staple food that is stored (*muqtat mudakhkhar*). According to him, among fruits of trees, it is only dates and raisins. The well-known position of his school is that *zakat* is obligatory on olives when their seed reaches five *awsuq* (the plural of *wasq*, a measure of about sixty *sa'*). It is taken from their oil after pressing, so its tenth or half-tenth is taken, as will come later. If their seed does not reach five *awsuq*, then there is no *zakat* on their oil according to him. The ruling on sesame, the seed of the red radish, and safflower is the ruling on olives in the well-known position of his school: their oil is taken if their seed reaches the threshold.

Al-Lakhmi said: the oil of one type is not combined with the oil of another due to the difference in their kinds. The well-known position of his school is that *zakat* is not obligatory on figs, though a group of his companions obligated it on them according to the principles of his school. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "I think Malik did not know that figs dry out, become staple food, and are stored. If he had known that, he would have made it like raisins, and he would not have counted it with the fruits that do not dry and are not stored, such as pomegranates and peaches. What is obligatory among the grains according to him is what is a staple and is stored, and that is: wheat, barley, *sult* (a kind of barley/wheat), *'alas* (emmer), millet, sorghum, rice, lentils, *julban* (a kind of chickpea), *lubiya* (black-eyed beans), sesame, lupine, fava beans, chickpeas, and *basilah* (a kind of pea)."

The well-known position of his school is that *kirsinnah* (a kind of fodder vetch) has no *zakat*, because it is fodder. From Ashhab, *zakat* is obligatory on it. It is among the legumes (*qitaniyy*) according to the well-known position of his school in the chapter on usury (*riba*), but not in the chapter on *zakat*.

It was said that it is *basilah*. According to Malik, all kinds of legumes are one kind with respect to *zakat*. So if someone harvests a *wasq* of fava beans, a *wasq* of chickpeas, another of lentils, another of *julban*, and another of *lubiya*, he must combine some of them with others and pay *zakat* from each of them according to its share. Likewise, according to him, wheat, barley, and *sult* are combined with one another as a single kind, and *zakat* is taken from each of them according to its share. According to him, dates are not combined with raisins, nor wheat with legumes, nor dates with wheat, nor any kind with another kind, except what we mentioned from him about combining (them) due to the closeness of benefit in them according to him. A single type, such as dates, raisins, and wheat, has its varieties combined with one another, such as *sayhani*, *barni*, *samra'* (a kind of wheat), *mahmulah* (a kind of wheat), black raisins, red raisins, and the like.

According to Malik, may God have mercy on him, there is no *zakat* on any fruit other than what we mentioned, such as pomegranates, apples, peaches, plums, pears, almonds, walnuts, citrons, and the like. Likewise, according to him, there is no *zakat* on any vegetables. He said in *al-Muwatta'*: "The Sunnah about which there is no disagreement among us, and what I heard from the people of knowledge, is that there is no charity (*sadaqah*) on any of the fruits at all: pomegranates, peaches, figs, and what is similar to them, and whatever is not similar to them if it is a fruit." He said: "Nor is there charity on fodder (*qadb*), nor on all herbs, nor on their prices if they are sold, until the year passes over their prices from the day they are sold and their owner receives their price while it is at the threshold." End of quotation from *al-Muwatta'*.

*Al-Firsik* (peach): with a kasra on the *fa'* and the *sin* with a sakin *ra'* between them, and ending with a *kaf*, it is the *khawkh* (plum/peach). It is a Yemeni dialect form. It was said: it is a type similar to it in size, smooth, unhairy, red and yellow, of good quality. It was also said: it is what does not split from its pit among the *khawkh*.

If the crop or the fruit is shared between two or more people, Malik said in *al-Muwatta'* about palm trees that are shared between two men, who cut eight *awsuq* of dates: there is no charity on them. And if one of them has what he cuts being five *awsuq*, and the other has what he cuts being four *awsuq* or less than that, on the same land, the charity is on the owner of the five *awsuq*, and there is no charity on the one who cut four *awsuq* or less. The practice is the same among all partners in every crop of grains that is harvested, or palm trees that are cut, or vineyards that are picked. If each of them cuts five *awsuq* of dates, or picks five *awsuq* of raisins, or harvests five *awsuq* of wheat, then *zakat* is due on him, and whoever has less than five *awsuq* has no charity on him. Charity is obligatory only on the one whose cutting, picking, or harvest reaches five *awsuq*. End of quotation from Malik's *al-Muwatta'*, may God have mercy on him.

If he keeps that grain or those dates after paying their *zakat* for years and then sells them, then the ruling according to Malik is what he mentioned in his *Muwatta'*, where he said: "The Sunnah among us is that for all of these kinds whose *zakat* has been paid, wheat, dates, raisins, and all grains, if their owner keeps them after paying his charity for years and then sells them, there is no *zakat* on their price until a year passes over their price from the day he sells them, provided that the origin of those kinds was from profit or something else, and that it was not for trade. This is like food, grains, and goods that a man acquires, then keeps for years, then sells for gold or silver: there is no *zakat* on their price until a year passes over it from the day he sells it. But if the origin of those goods was for trade, then its owner owes *zakat* on them when he sells them, if he held them for a year from the day he paid *zakat* on the wealth with which he bought them." End of quotation from *al-Muwatta'*. This applies to the hoarder (*muhtakir*). As for the one who rotates goods for trade (*mudir*), he values them after a year from his *zakat*, as in *al-Mudawwanah* from Ibn al-Qasim.

This is the summary of the position of Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) regarding what zakat is obligatory upon among fruits and grains. The position of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) is that zakat is not obligatory on any of the fruits of trees either, except what is a staple food that is stored (yudda'ar). According to him, this applies only to dates and raisins, as already mentioned from Malik. According to him, zakat is not obligatory on other fruits such as figs, apples, quince, pomegranates, and the like, because they are not staple foods nor stored wealth. Nor is zakat obligatory according to him on talh al-fuhhal (the male palm flower), because fruit does not come from it.

His opinion differs regarding olives. In the older opinion (al-qadim), he said zakat is obligatory on them, based on what is narrated from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he set a tenth (ushr) on oil, and from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "On olives there is zakat." In the newer opinion (al-jadid), he said: there is no zakat on olives, because they are not a staple food, so they are like vegetables.

* *

Al-Shafi'i's opinion also differed regarding al-wars (safflower/saffron-like dye plant). In the older opinion he said zakat is obligatory on it, based on what is narrated that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) wrote to the Banu Khuffash: "Pay the zakat of maize and wars." In the newer opinion he said: there is no zakat on it, because it is a plant that is not eaten as a staple, so it resembles vegetables. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: whoever says there is no ushr on wars does not make it obligatory on saffron; whoever says it is obligatory on wars, it is possible he would make it obligatory on saffron, because both are fragrant (tayyib); and it is possible he would not make it obligatory on saffron, and differentiate between them, on the basis that wars is a tree with a trunk, whereas saffron is a plant.

His opinion also differed regarding honey. In the older opinion he said: it is possible that it is obligatory upon it, and its basis is what is narrated that the Banu Shababa, a clan of Fahm, used to pay to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the bees they had, one-tenth, from every ten jars one jar. In the newer opinion he said: it is not obligatory, because it is not a staple food, so a tenth is not obligatory upon it, like eggs.

His opinion also differed regarding al-qurtum, which is the seed of safflower (al-usfur). In the older opinion he said it is obligatory if the hadith of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) is authentic. In the newer opinion he said it is not obligatory, because it is not a staple food, so it resembles vegetables. All of this was stated by the author of al-Muhadhdhab. Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: the report narrated from Umar, that "he set a tenth on oil," is weak; al-Bayhaqi narrated it and said: its chain is interrupted (munqati'), and its narrator is not strong. He said: the most authentic thing narrated concerning olives is the statement of al-Zuhri: "The sunnah has passed concerning the zakat of olives: that it is taken from the one who presses his olives at the time of pressing; for what is watered by rain or is rain-fed (ba'l), a tenth; and for what is irrigated by the splashing of a water-wheel (nadih), half a tenth." This is a mawquf report whose wide currency is not known, and it is not used as proof according to the sound view.

Al-Bayhaqi said: the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (may Allah be pleased with them both) is higher in rank and more deserving to be acted upon, meaning their narration that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them both when he sent them to Yemen: "Do not take charity except from these four kinds: barley, wheat, dates, and raisins."

As for the report mentioned from Ibn Abbas, it is also weak. The report mentioned from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) is also weak; al-Shafi'i mentioned it and declared it weak, as did others, and the hadith scholars agreed on its weakness, and our companions agreed in the books of the school on its weakness. Al-Bayhaqi said: no chain has been established in this matter that can serve as proof. He said: the original state is the absence of obligation, so there is no zakat on what no sound hadith has been reported about, or what is in the meaning of what a sound hadith has been reported about. As for the hadith of the Banu Shababa concerning honey, Abu Dawud, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated it through 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father, from his grandfather, with a weak chain. al-Tirmidhi said in his Jami': nothing great is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this matter. Al-Bayhaqi said: al-Tirmidhi said in the book al-'Ilal: al-Bukhari said: there is nothing authentic concerning the zakat of honey.

So the conclusion is that all the reports and hadiths in this section are weak. End of al-Nawawi's words.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis, concerning the report of Umar mentioned about olives: al-Bayhaqi narrated it with an interrupted chain, and its narrator, 'Uthman ibn 'Ata', is weak. He said: the most authentic thing in the chapter is the statement of Ibn Shihab: "The sunnah has passed concerning the zakat of olives," etc.

Ibn Hajar also said in al-Talkhis, concerning the report of Ibn Abbas mentioned about olives: the author of al-Muhadhdhab mentioned it from Ibn Abbas, and al-Nawawi declared it weak; Ibn Abi Shaybah also narrated it, and in its chain is Layth ibn Abi Sulaym.

Ibn Hajar also said: al-Hakim narrated in the history of Nishapur through the route of 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, traced to the Prophet: "Zakat is on five: on wheat, barley, grapes, palm trees, and olives." In its chain is 'Uthman ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, who is al-Waqqasi: matruk al-hadith (abandoned in narration).

Ibn Hajar said concerning the report mentioned from Abu Bakr, that he used to take zakat from the seed of safflower, which is al-qurtum: "I have not found any origin for it."

Ibn Hajar also said in al-Talkhis, concerning the report of the Prophet (ﷺ) taking zakat on honey: al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On honey, from every ten skins (azqaq), one skin (ziqq)." He said: there is discussion about its chain, and it is not authentic; in its chain is Sadaqah al-Samin, who has weak memory.

It has been opposed. al-Nasa'i said: this is a munkar hadith. al-Bayhaqi narrated it and said: Sadaqah alone narrated it, and he is weak; Talhah ibn Zayd followed him, from Musa ibn Yasar. al-Marwazi mentioned it, and it is reported from Ahmad that he declared it weak. al-Tirmidhi mentioned that he asked al-Bukhari about it, and he said: it is from Nafi', from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a mursal (report). al-Hakim, in the history of Nishapur, quoted from Abu Hatim, from his father, who said: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Dhuhli narrated a hadith that nearly destroyed him: he narrated from 'Arim, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Usama ibn Zayd, from his father, from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet: "A tenth was taken from honey."

Abu Hatim said: it is actually from Usama ibn Zayd, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather in the same way; 'Arim and others narrated it to us. He said: perhaps 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb dropped out of his book, and this error entered it.

al-Tirmidhi said: and in the chapter there is also a report from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr. I say: Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated it through the route of 'Amr ibn al-Harith al-Misri, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "Hilal, one of the Banu Mut'an, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the tenths of his bees, and asked him to protect a valley of his called Salaba, so he protected it for him. When Umar became ruler, he wrote to Sufyan ibn Wahb: if he pays you what he used to pay to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the tenths of his bees, then protect Salaba for him; otherwise it is merely the fly of rain that whoever wishes may eat."

al-Daraqutni said: it is narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith and Ibn Lahi'a, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, as a musnad (connected) report; and Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari narrated it from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb as a mursal, from Umar as a mursal. I say: this is its defect; 'Abd al-Rahman and Ibn Lahi'a are not of the people of precision, but 'Amr ibn al-Harith, one of the trustworthy narrators, followed them, and Usama ibn Zayd followed them from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb in Ibn Majah and others, as has passed.

al-Tirmidhi said: and in the chapter there is also a report from Abu Sayyara. I say: he is al-Mut'i. He said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, I have bees. He said: pay the tenths. I said: O Messenger of Allah, protect its mountain for me." Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Bayhaqi narrated it through the route of Sulayman ibn Musa from Abu Sayyara, and it is interrupted (munqati').

al-Bukhari said: Sulayman did not meet any of the Companions, and there is nothing authentic concerning the zakat of honey. Abu 'Umar said: no proof is established by this. He said: and from Abu Hurayra. I say: al-Bayhaqi narrated it, and in its chain is 'Abdullah ibn Muharrar, who is matruk. He also narrated it from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Dhubab: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) appointed him over his people, and he said to them: 'Pay the tenth on honey.'" Umar came with it, took it, sold it, and then placed it in the charities of the Muslims. In its chain is Muni' ibn 'Abdullah, whom al-Bukhari, al-Azdi and others declared weak.

al-Shafi'i said: Sa'd ibn Abi Dhubab relates what indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not command anything concerning it, and that it was something he himself saw, and his people volunteered it for him. Al-Za'farani narrated from al-Shafi'i: the hadith that there is a tenth on honey is weak, and my choice is that nothing is taken from it. al-Bukhari said: nothing authentic is reported on it. Ibn al-Mundhir said: there is nothing established on it. In the Muwatta' from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr, who said: "The letter of Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz came to my father while he was at Mina: that you should not take charity from horses or from honey." End of Ibn Hajar's words verbatim.

Ibn Hajar also said in al-Talkhis: the hadith of Mu'adh, that he did not take zakat on honey, and that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not command me concerning it with anything," was narrated by Abu Dawud in al-Marasil, al-Humaydi in his Musnad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and al-Bayhaqi through the route of Tawus from him. There is an interruption between Tawus and Mu'adh, but al-Bayhaqi said: it is strong, because Tawus was knowledgeable about the judgments of Mu'adh.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: there is no doubt that paying its zakat is more cautious, and this is the school of Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him), and the author of al-Mughni transmitted it from Makhul, al-Zuhri, Sulayman ibn Musa, al-Awza'i and Ishaq.

Their proof is the hadiths you have seen. There is nothing on it according to Malik, al-Shafi'i in his newer opinion, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ibn al-Mundhir and others.

Their proof is that nothing reported about it is authentic, and that the original state is the freedom of the liability (bara'at al-dhimmah), and that it is a liquid that exits from an animal, so it resembles milk.

Abu Hanifa said: if it is in land subject to 'ushr, then zakat is due on it; otherwise there is no zakat on it. The nisab of honey is said to be five faraq, which is the view of al-Zuhri; it is said to be five awsuq, and this is the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad.

Abu Hanifa said: zakat is due on its little and its much, and the faraq is sixteen ratls by the Iraqi measure; it is said sixty ratls; it is said one hundred and twenty ratls; it is said three sa'; and it is said other than that. This was stated in al-Mughni.

As for grains: according to al-Shafi'i, zakat is not obligatory except on what is eaten as a staple and stored from them. According to him there is no zakat on any of the fruits that are neither eaten as staples nor stored, nor on any vegetables. So his school agrees with the school of Malik, as we have mentioned, except that al-Shafi'i does not combine some types with others, whereas Malik combines the pulses (qatani) with one another for zakat; likewise wheat, barley and sult, as has passed.

* *

As for the school of Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him), it is that zakat is obligatory on what the earth produces, of what dries and remains, of what is measured by volume (yukal). The descriptive attributes of what is zakatable according to him among what the earth produces are three: measurement (al-kayl), durability (al-baqa'), and dryness (al-yubs). So whatever is like this among grains and fruits is obligatory upon according to him, whether it is a staple or not; and whatever is not like this is not obligatory upon. Thus zakat is obligatory according to him on wheat, barley, sult, rice, maize, millet (al-dukhn), and pulses such as broad beans (al-baqila), lentils, and chickpeas; on spices such as cumin, caraway, and seeds such as flaxseed, cucumber and cucumber seeds, and cucurbit seeds, and seeds of herbs such as rashad (garden cress), radish seeds, al-qurtum, sesame, and the like of all other grains. Likewise it is obligatory according to him on fruits which combine the stated attributes, such as dates, raisins, almonds, pistachios, and hazelnuts. And there is no zakat according to him on any fruits such as peaches, apricots, pears, apples, figs, and walnuts, nor on any vegetables such as cucumbers, cucumbers, eggplant, turnips, carrots, and the like.

Something similar to what we have mentioned is narrated from Ahmad concerning grains, from 'Ata', Abu Yusuf and Muhammad. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid said: there is nothing due on spices (al-abazir), on seeds (al-bazr), or on the seeds of herbs (habb al-buqul).

The author of al-Mughni said: "Perhaps he holds that zakat is due only on what is a staple (qut) or a condiment (adam), because what lies beyond these has no explicit text and is not in the meaning of what is textually stated, so it remains under the original negation (al-nafy al-asli)." In the well-known position of Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him), there is no zakat on what grows wild on permissible land that is not owned except by taking it, such as buTm (the terebinth or bitter nut), wild barley (sha'ir al-jabal), the seeds of qutuna, the seeds of the buqla (purslane), habb al-namam, the seeds of ushnan (a saltwort), and similar things. From al-Qadi, it is reported that zakat is due on it if it grows on one's land.

The sound view is the first. If a grain such as wheat, for example, falls on one's land and sprouts, zakat is due on it, because he owns it. Zakat is not due on what is neither a grain nor a fruit, whether or not it is measurable (yukal) and storable ( idikhar). Thus it is not due on leaves such as the leaves of the lote tree (sidr), khatmi (marshmallow), ushnan, sa'tar (thyme), myrtle (ās), and the like, because these are not explicitly mentioned nor in the meaning of what is mentioned. Nor is there zakat in his view on flowers such as saffron, safflower (al-'usfur), and cotton, because they are neither grains nor fruits, nor are they measured by volume; so zakat is not due on them, like vegetables.

Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "There is nothing on cotton," and he said: "There is no zakat on saffron." This is the apparent meaning of the words of al-Kharaqi and the preference of Abu Bakr, as stated by Ibn Qudama in al-Mughni.

The narrations from Ahmad differ concerning olives. His son Salih narrated from him that zakat is due on them, but it was also narrated from him that there is no zakat on them. This is the preference of Abu Bakr, and the apparent meaning of al-Kharaqi's words implies it, as the author of al-Mughni also stated.

As for Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), he holds that zakat is due on everything the earth produces, whether food or otherwise. Abu Yusuf said on his authority: except firewood, grass, reeds, straw, palm fronds, dharira reed, and sugar cane. End of quote. The dharira is a reed brought from India, like the reed of arrows, red in color, used as medicine. Among those who said the same as Abu Hanifa is al-Nakha'i, and something similar was narrated from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. It is also the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, the teacher of Abu Hanifa, and Ibn al-'Arabi al-Maliki supported it in his Ahkam, saying: "As for Abu Hanifa, he made the verse a mirror, and so he saw the truth."

This is the summary of the positions of the four Imams (may Allah be pleased with them) regarding what zakat is due on from what the earth produces. We will indicate, if Allah wills, the evidence of each of them for what he held.

As for Abu Hanifa: he argued for the obligation of zakat on everything the earth produces, in small or large quantity, by the generality of this noble verse which we are discussing, since Allah says in it: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-An'am: 141], and by the generality of His saying: ﴿O you who believe, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 267], and by the generality of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "On what the sky waters, a tenth." He did not accept specifying it by the hadith: "There is no charity on less than five wasq." This is because the established principle in his jurisprudential methodology (usul), may Allah have mercy on him, is that the general term (al-'amm) is definitive in its inclusiveness, and it applies to all its individual members, as he indicated in Marāqī al-Su'ud in his words:

It indicates each individual with certainty, but comprehensiveness is not certain;
Rather, according to most scholars it is by preponderance, and the definitive view is the school of al-Nu'man.

So whatever is less than five wasq enters his understanding definitively into the generality of the aforementioned verses and hadith. Therefore, for him, the general is not specified by the particular; rather, they conflict, and giving precedence to what indicates obligation is better than giving precedence to what indicates otherwise, for caution in discharging the obligation of the demand.

As for Malik and al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on them both), their argument for their view that there is no zakat except on the date palm and the grape among trees, and on no grain except what is eaten as a staple and stored, and that there is no zakat on fruits or vegetables, is that the text and the consensus (ijma') indicate that zakat is obligatory on wheat, barley, dates, and raisins, and each of these is a staple and storable. So they attached to them everything that has the same meaning, because it is a staple and storable. They did not see that among trees there is any staple or storable item other than dates and raisins; so no other fruits share the same cause (illa). For this reason, a group of Malik's followers said that figs are obligatory according to the principles of Malik's school, because they are like raisins in being a staple and storable.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "The apparent meaning is that Malik did not know that figs were like that. As for grains, staple and storable qualities are found in them, so they (Malik and al-Shafi'i) attached to wheat and barley everything that is a staple and storable, such as rice, maize, millet, legumes, and the like. This is an analogy (ilhaq) by them, may Allah have mercy on them both, of the unmentioned case to the mentioned case, by the common cause, which in their view is being a staple and storable, because being a staple and storable is suitable for the obligation of charity in it, since the poor need a food they can eat and store."

As for Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him), his argument for his position is that zakat is due on what endures, dries, and can be measured, whereas what does not dry and does not last, such as fruits and vegetables, was not taken as zakat in his time (ﷺ) nor in the time of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

His evidence for requiring measurement is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no charity on less than five wasq." He said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) clarified that the place of the obligation is in the wasq, and this is specific to what is measured, as will be explained, if Allah wills."

As for the evidence of the majority, namely Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them), that there is no zakat on fruits and vegetables, it is clear: vegetables were very abundant in Medina, and fruits were abundant in al-Ta'if, yet it is not reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) nor from any of his Companions that he took zakat from any of these.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse: "In al-Ta'if there were pomegranates, peaches, and citrons, yet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not object to them, nor did he mention them, nor did any of his successors." I say: this, although he did not mention it in al-Ahkam, is the correct position on the issue, and that there is nothing on vegetables. As for the verse, it has been disputed whether it is muhkam (definitive and operative), or mansukh (abrogated), or to be understood as recommended (nadb). No decisive evidence settles which of these meanings is intended. Rather, the decisive known matter is what Ibn Bukayr mentioned in his Ahkam: that Kufa was conquered after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and after the rulings had been settled in Medina. Could anyone imagine, or anyone with even a little insight, that a law like this was left unimplemented in the abode of emigration (Dar al-Hijra) and the place where revelation settled, and even in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, until the people of Kufa acted upon it? Truly, this is a great calamity for whoever thinks this or says it.

I say: among what indicates this from the meaning of the revelation is His saying: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67]. Do you think he would conceal anything he was commanded to convey or to explain? Far be it from him. And He says: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. And from the perfection of the religion is that he did not take anything from vegetables.

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, as narrated by al-Daraqutni: "The melon crops used to yield for us ten thousand (units), and there was nothing in them (no zakat)." Al-Zuhri and al-Hasan said: the price of vegetables is zakatable when they ripen and the price reaches two hundred dirhams, and al-Awza'i said the same concerning the price of fruits. But there is no proof in their view against what we have mentioned.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Mu'adh that he wrote to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him about vegetables, which are the buqul, and he said: "There is nothing in them." This meaning has also been narrated from Jabir, Anas, 'Ali, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, Abu Musa, and 'A'isha; al-Daraqutni (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned their hadiths. Al-Tirmidhi said: "Nothing authentic is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this subject." Some of Abu Hanifa's followers (may Allah have mercy on him) argued with the hadith of Salih ibn Musa from Mansur, from Ibrahim, from al-Aswad, from 'A'isha, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On what the earth produces of vegetables there is zakat." Abu 'Umar said: "No reliable transmitter from the students of Mansur narrated this in this form; it is rather a saying of Ibrahim."

I say: when the argument from the Sunna falls because its chains are weak, nothing remains except what we have mentioned, namely specifying the generality of the verse and the generality of His saying (ﷺ): "On what the sky waters, a tenth," by what we have mentioned. End of al-Qurtubi's words.

The argument of those who said there is no zakat except on the four agreed-upon items, namely wheat, barley, dates, and raisins, is the hadiths we presented at the beginning of this discussion, among which is the hadith of Mu'adh and Abu Musa, which al-Bayhaqi said is strong and connected (muttasil).

Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: there is no zakat on any vegetable except that which has a lasting fruit (thamara baqiya). Except for saffron and the like, which are weighed (yuzan), for which there is zakat. Muhammad took into account safflower, flax, and seeds: when the seeds of safflower and flax reach five wasq, then safflower and flax follow the seeds, and a tenth or half a tenth is taken from them. As for cotton, there is nothing on it for less than five loads (ahmal), and a load is three hundred 'Iraqi ratls. For woad (al-wars) and saffron, there is nothing for less than five manns of them, and when either reaches five manns, charity is due on it. Abu Yusuf said: likewise sugar cane from which sugar is made, which grows in tithe land (ard al-'ushr) rather than kharaj land; on it is what is on saffron.

Ibn al-Majishun (ʿAbd al-Malik) required zakat on the roots of fruit trees but not on herbs, and this contradicts what the school of his own madhhab, Malik and his companions, held. Thus al-Qurtubi said.

Note

Whoever says there is no zakat on pomegranates, which is the majority of scholars, and whoever says there is no zakat on olives, the position of each of them necessarily implies that the verse we are discussing, which is His saying: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾, is either abrogated or intended for something other than zakat. This is because, if it is definitive and refers to the obligatory zakat, it is impossible to hold that there is no zakat on olives and pomegranates alongside it, since it explicitly includes them, for the things mentioned in His saying: ﴿And He it is who brought into being gardens, trellised and untrellised, and the date palm and crops of varying flavor, and the olive and pomegranate, similar and dissimilar﴾, the pronoun in His saying: ﴿Eat of its fruit﴾ [al-An'am: 141] and His saying: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ refers to all of them, as is clear without ambiguity. Thus the olive and pomegranate enter it by a primary entry about which there is no doubt. So the view of most scholars that there is no zakat on pomegranates strengthens the view that the verse was abrogated, or that it refers to other than the obligatory zakat. And Allah knows best.

It is reported from Abu Yusuf that he required zakat on henna (hina'). Know that the school of Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Zahiri on this issue is very strong from the standpoint of reasoning. He said: what the earth produces is of two kinds: wasq-able (mawsaq) and non-wasq-able (ghayr mawsaq). What is wasq-able, zakat is due on what reaches five wasq, by His saying (ﷺ): "There is no charity on less than five wasq, and no zakat on less than that from it." What is not wasq-able, zakat is due on its small and large quantity, by the generality of His saying (ﷺ): "On what the sky waters, a tenth." It is not specified by the hadith: "There is no charity on less than five wasq," because it is not wasq-able at all.

The author, may Allah pardon him, said: This view is the most consistent with the apparent meaning of the texts, and it contains a kind of reconciliation between them. However, it is refuted by what we have already mentioned: that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not address vegetables despite their abundance in Madinah, nor fruits despite their abundance in al-Ta'if. Had the general wording included them, he (ﷺ) would have explained it. And when you know the statements of the scholars on determining what zakat is obligatory upon, and the evidence for their positions that we have mentioned,

Know that the majority of scholars said: zakat is not obligatory except on five wasqs (a wasq being a measure of sixty sa') or more, based on his saying (ﷺ): "There is no charity on what is less than five wasqs," the hadith. It was narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), and by Muslim from the hadith of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him).

Among those who held this view are the three Imams: Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them), and their companions. It is also the view of Ibn 'Umar, Jabir, Abu Umamah ibn Sahl, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Makhul, al-Hakam, al-Nakha'i, the people of Madinah, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and the rest of the people of knowledge, as Ibn Qudamah and others reported from them.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: "We know of no one who disagreed on this except Abu Hanifah and those who followed him, and Mujahid." All scholars have agreed that the wasq is sixty sa'. It may be pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the waw, and the fatha is more well known and more eloquent. It was said that with a kasra it is a noun, and with a fatha it is a verbal noun. Its plural for small numbers is awsuq and awsaq, and for large numbers wusuq.

Know that the sa' is four mudds (a mudd being a unit of volume) by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). The mudd, approximately, is the filling of two medium hands, neither clenched nor fully spread out. Its precise measurement by weight is one and a third ritls by the Baghdadi ritl. Thus the total of five wasqs in mudds is one thousand two hundred mudds, and in sa's it is three hundred. By weight, this is one thousand six hundred ritls. The ritl is the weight of one hundred and twenty-eight Meccan dirhams. Some scholars added four-sevenths of a dirham, each dirham being the weight of fifty and two-fifths grains of ordinary barley, as the scholars of the Malikis verified. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) is among the people most knowledgeable of the true nature of the mudd and the sa', as is well known. It was said about it other than what we have mentioned.

As for the third ruling among the rulings of this third issue mentioned at the beginning of this discussion, which is determining the amount that must be paid, there is no disagreement among the scholars about it. It is one tenth on what is not irrigated with hardship, such as what is watered by rain, a river, or whose roots reach the water in the ground. As for what is irrigated by a machine, such as what is watered by water-wheels (nawadih), it is one twentieth. This is established from him (ﷺ) through the hadith of Jabir and Ibn 'Umar. If a field is sometimes watered by the sky's rain and sometimes by a water-wheel, then if both are equal, the obligation is three-quarters of a tenth, with no disagreement among the scholars. If one of the two is predominant, it was said that the greater is considered and the lesser follows it. This was the view of Ahmad, Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, and 'Ata', and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. It was also said that it is assessed proportionally. Each of these two views was made prominent by some Malikis. Some of them reported a narration from Malik: that the criterion is what the crop is sustained by and completes. Among the Hanbalis, those who held the proportional view include Ibn Hamid. If the amount is unknown, the tenth is obligatory as a precaution, as Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah have mercy on him) stated in the narration of 'Abd Allah. This was said in al-Mughni, and he gave the reason that the original rule is the obligation of a tenth, and half of it falls away only upon the certainty of hardship. If the reason for reduction is not established, the original ruling remains, and this is very clear. If the collector (al-sa'i) and the owner of the property disagree about which of the two they irrigated more with, then the owner's word is accepted without oath, because people are not made to swear over their charities. There is no waqs (the exempt portion) in grains and fruits. Rather, whatever exceeds the nisab (minimum threshold) is paid from it in proportion.

Issues related to this discussion:

The first issue: We have already mentioned the consensus of the scholars on the obligation of zakat on dates and raisins. The majority hold that they are estimated (kharš, estimation by assessment) when their ripeness appears, because the owners need to eat the fresh dates and grapes. For this reason, the estimation of dates and grapes was prescribed. Each of them is estimated tree by tree, until the quantity of wasqs in the whole is known at present. Then the amount that dehydration will reduce is deducted from it. If there are five wasqs of grapes or fresh dates, and when dried it becomes four wasqs, for example, then there is no zakat on it, because the nisab is measured by dried dates and raisins, not by fresh dates and grapes. When it has been estimated in the manner we have described, the owners are left in control of it. After harvesting, they bring the amount of zakat, in dates or raisins, according to the aforementioned estimate. By this, both caution for the poor and leniency toward the owners of the fruit are achieved. If a calamity (jā'iḥa, a sudden destructive loss) strikes it after the estimation, it is taken into account, and the zakat on what the calamity destroyed falls away. If five wasqs or more remain after it, he pays the zakat; otherwise he does not. There is no disagreement among the scholars about considering the calamity after the estimation.

Among those who held that palm trees and vines are estimated were the three Imams: Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on them); 'Umar ibn al-Khattab; Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah; Marwan; al-Qasim ibn Muhammad; al-Hasan; 'Ata'; al-Zuhri; 'Amr ibn Dinar; 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi al-Makhariq; Abu 'Ubayd; Abu Thawr; and most of the people of knowledge, as Ibn Qudamah reported from them in al-Mughni. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that estimation is an innovation (bid'ah). Al-Thawri prohibited it. Abu Hanifah and his companions said: estimation is conjecture and guesswork by which no ruling is binding. Estimation was only a means of frightening those who guard the fruit, so that they would not cheat. As for it being binding as a ruling, it is not.

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: It should not be hidden that this view is refuted by the clear and authentic texts of the Sunnah. Among them is what the two Shaykhs recorded in their Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the expedition of Tabuk, and we came to Wadi al-Qura, to a garden belonging to a woman. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Estimate it.' So we estimated it, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) estimated it at ten wasqs, and said: 'Keep count of it until we return to you, if Allah wills.' We set off until we came to Tabuk," and he mentioned the hadith.

He said: "Then we returned until we came to Wadi al-Qura, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the woman about her garden (p-510): how much did its fruit amount to? She said: It amounted to ten wasqs." This hadith, agreed upon by the two Shaykhs, is clear evidence for the legitimacy of estimation, as you see.

And from 'Attab ibn Asid (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to send someone to the people to estimate their vines and fruits for them." It was recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Hibban.

And from 'Attab (may Allah be pleased with him) also, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that grapes be estimated just as palm trees are estimated, and their zakat be taken in raisins just as the charity of palm trees is taken in dates." It was also recorded by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, and al-Daraqutni.

The verification regarding this hadith of 'Attab is that it is among the mursal reports (hadiths where the Successor omits the Companion from the chain) of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him), because he did not meet 'Attab. Sa'id was born during the caliphate of 'Umar, and 'Attab died on the day Abu Bakr died (may Allah be pleased with them both). Many of those who deny the validity of mursal reports have nevertheless established proof by the mursal reports of Sa'id. Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "Some of our companions said that the mursal reports of Ibn al-Musayyib are accepted without qualification. The more correct view is that his mursal reports are accepted only when they are supported by one of four things: that it is narrated with a full chain (musnad) by another route; that it is transmitted as a mursal from another route; that some of the Companions hold it; or that most of the scholars hold it. All of this exists here, for the scholars among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them agreed on the obligation of zakat on dates and raisins."

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: From what al-Nawawi mentioned, you know that the Shafi'is agree on accepting this mursal report, and the three Imams accept mursal reports without qualification. Thus, the consensus of the four schools has become evident on accepting a mursal report like this one. Al-Daraqutni narrated this hadith with a chain containing al-Waqidi, connected, saying: from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, from 'Attab ibn Asid.

And from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to send 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, and he would estimate the palm trees when they became ripe, before they were eaten from. Then he would give the Jews the choice: they could take them at that estimate, or hand them over to them at that estimate, so that he could compute the zakat before the fruits were eaten and distributed." It was recorded by Ahmad and Abu Dawud. It has been criticized on the grounds that there is an intermediary between Ibn Jurayj and al-Zuhri who is unknown. 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Daraqutni narrated it without the intermediary mentioned. Ibn Jurayj is a mudallis (one who conceals defects in his chain), so perhaps he omitted it by tadlis. This was said by Ibn Hajar. He said: al-Daraqutni mentioned the disagreement regarding it. He said: Salih ibn Abi al-Akhdar narrated it from al-Zuhri, from Ibn al-Musayyib, from Abu Hurayrah, while Ma'mar, Malik, and 'Aqil narrated it as a mursal and did not mention Abu (p-511) Hurayrah. Abu Dawud recorded through the route of Ibn Jurayj: Abu al-Zubayr informed me that he heard Jabir say: "Ibn Rawahah estimated it at forty thousand wasqs."

Ibn Hajar also said in al-Talkhis: Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sent 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah to Khaybar to estimate for them," the hadith.

Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated from the hadith of Jabir: "When Allah granted His Messenger the conquest of Khaybar, he left them in it and made it shared between himself and them. He sent 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, and he estimated it for them," the hadith. Ibn Majah narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Daraqutni narrated from Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent his father as an estimator, and a man came and said: O Messenger of Allah, Abu Hathmah has overestimated against me," the hadith. Then Ibn Hajar mentioned the hadith of 'Attab and the hadith of 'A'isha, which we have already cited. Then he said: "And in the Companions, by Abu Nu'aym, through the route of al-Salt ibn Zubayd ibn al-Salt, from his father, from his grandfather: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed him over the estimation, and he said: Let us have half, and leave them half, for they steal, and we cannot reach them.'"

From all that we have mentioned, you know that estimation is a established ruling from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), not a false conjecture or guesswork. Rather, it is an ijtihad (independent reasoning) that the Sharia has brought regarding determining the quantity of fruit. Its determination by estimation is a type of measure and standard, so it is like the valuation of destroyed property. The time of estimation is when the ripeness of the fruit appears, as we mentioned earlier, based on the narration we cited: "that he (ﷺ) used to send the estimator, who would estimate the palm trees for them when they became ripe, before they were eaten." There is no disagreement among the scholars on this.

The scholars who held that estimation is valid differed about its ruling. It was said: it is a sunnah, because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to command it. It was also said: it is obligatory, based on his saying in the hadith of 'Attab, which we mentioned earlier: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded that grapes be estimated," the hadith. They said: the command implies obligation. Also, if one neglects estimation, some of the poor's right may be lost. The more apparent view is that it is not obligatory, because ruling that this command is obligatory, such that abandoning it deserves punishment, requires a clear and strong proof. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 141 (part 5 of 6):

The scholars who hold the view of estimation (khars) disagreed over whether the estimator (al-khāris) should leave something behind for the owner. Some scholars said: he must leave a third or a quarter. This is based on what Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan (except Ibn Majah) related, as did Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, from Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you estimate, take [your share], and leave a third. If you do not leave a third, then leave a quarter." If it is objected that its chain contains Abd al-Rahman ibn Mas'ud ibn Niyar, the narrator from Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, and al-Bazzar said that he was the only one to narrate it, and Ibn al-Qattan said: "His condition is not known," the answer is that it has a corroborating report with a chain agreed upon as sound: that Umar ibn al-Khattab ordered it, as al-Hakim stated. Among its corroborations is what Ibn Abd al-Barr related from Jabir in a marfu' report: "Be lenient in estimation," the hadith; and its chain contains Ibn Lahi'ah.

Among those who held this view were Imam Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Layth, Abu Ubayd, and others. The well-known position of the Maliki school is this, while the sound position in the Shafi'i school is that the estimator does not leave anything behind.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The view that he leaves a third or a quarter is the correct one, because the hadith is established, and al-Hakim and Ibn Hibban declared it sound, and nothing that contradicts it has been established. Also, people need to eat and to feed their neighbours, their guests, their friends, and those who ask; and because some of the dates fall, birds peck at them, and passersby eat from them.
