If the estimator leaves nothing for them, then the apparent meaning is that they may eat an amount equal to what would have been required to be dropped, and it is not counted against them.

This is the position of Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is what the aforementioned hadith indicates. If the fruit increases or decreases from what the estimator estimated, some scholars said: there is no zakat on the excess, and he is liable for the zakat on what is lacking, because this is a ruling that has already been issued.

Some said: it is recommended to pay on the excess, and the zakat on the deficit is not waived.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: As for what is between him and Allah, there is no doubt that he is not obliged to pay zakat on what did not exist. As for what is between him and the people, zakat may be obligatory on him. Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki said in his Mukhtasar: "If it exceeds the estimate of an expert, then paying is preferable, and is that on its apparent sense or obligatory? There are two interpretations."

Its commentator al-Mawwaq said, from the Mudawwana: Malik said: "Whoever is estimated at four awsuq and harvests five awsuq, I prefer that he pay zakat." Ibn Yunus said: Some of our shaykhs said: the word "I prefer" here is meant as an obligation, and this is correct, like a judge who issues a ruling and then it becomes clear that it was a plain error. Ibn Arafa said: most scholars took it this way, while Ibn Rushd and Iyad took it as recommendation.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: That zakat is obligatory on the excess is the more evident view, most Malikis hold it, and it is the sound view among the Shafi'is. As for the deficit: if it is proven by evidence that the fruit fell short of what was estimated, then the apparent meaning is that the zakat on the shortfall is waived, even if the owner claims the estimator erred.

Some people of knowledge said: his claim is not accepted, because the estimator is trustworthy. Some scholars said: his claim of the estimator's error is accepted if it is plausible; but if it is far-fetched, such as claiming an excess of half or two-thirds, then his word is not accepted in any of it. This detailed distinction is the position of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, except that some Shafi'is said: he is relieved of the zakat on the portion of the large amount that he claimed as the deficit to which his claim is accepted. But if he claims that the estimator wronged him deliberately, his claim is not accepted against him, without disagreement, just as if he claimed the ruler's injustice or the witness's lying. Likewise, if he claims that the estimator erred in the estimate but does not specify the amount of the excess, it is not accepted from him; the Shafi'i scholars explicitly stated this. If the owner of the fruit claims that a calamity struck it and destroyed part of it, the apparent meaning is that he is believed regarding what is plausible for his claim, just as if he claimed that part of it was stolen at night for example; it is said that he takes an oath.

It is also said: No, even if he attributes the destruction of the fruit to a cause that the senses contradict, such as saying: "It was destroyed by a fire that broke out on the threshing floor at such-and-such a time," and we know that it did not burn at that time, his words are not heeded. If the mentioned cause is known to have occurred and its effect was general, he is believed without an oath; if he is suspected, he takes an oath. It is said: an oath is obligatory; it is said: it is recommended. If neither the absence nor the existence of the mentioned cause is known, the sound view is that he is required to provide evidence that the underlying cause existed, and then his word is accepted regarding the destruction by it. This final distinction is the Shafi'i position, which al-Nawawi mentioned in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, and its rationale is clear. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Most scholars hold that only dates and raisins are estimated, so olives, grain, and other things are not estimated. Some scholars permitted it for olives, and some permitted it for all grains.

The sound view is that it is not permitted except for dates and grapes, for three reasons:

First: the text indicating estimation was revealed only concerning these two, as previously mentioned in the hadith of Attab ibn Asid and other hadiths.

Second: other things are not in the same category as these two, because the need to eat fresh dates before they become dates, and grapes before they become raisins, is common, and other things are not like this.

Third: the fruit of the palm is visible and gathered in its clusters, and grapes are likewise visible and gathered in their bunches, so guarding them is possible, unlike other things, for grain is scattered over its plants, and crops are hidden in their ears.

(p-514) The apparent view is that what people customarily need to eat is not counted, for the reasons we have mentioned. The Malikis said: whatever they eat of the grain is counted against them, but what animals eat during threshing is not counted.

* *

The second issue: it is not permitted to pay the zakat on fruit except from dried dates and dried raisins; likewise, the zakat on grain may be paid only from dry grain after it has been cleaned. There is no disagreement among scholars on this. The cost of tending the fruit and grain until they dry and are cleaned is paid from the pure wealth of the owner of the fruit or crop. If someone pays the zakat on dates as unripe dates (busr) or fresh dates (rutab), or pays the zakat on raisins as grapes, it does not suffice for him, because he has paid something other than what is obligatory, since what is obligatory is dry dates and dry raisins by consensus.

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: If the one paying with fresh dates is the owner of the property, it does not suffice for him, and he is obliged to pay the surplus after drying, because he paid something other than the obligation, so it does not suffice, just as if he paid a young animal in place of mature animals. This is a clear text from him that fresh dates are not what is obligatory, and that their status relative to dates, which are what is obligatory, is like the status of young livestock relative to mature livestock, which are what is obligatory in livestock zakat.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, and his exact words are: If he pays fresh dates and grapes immediately, it does not suffice for him, without disagreement; and if the collector takes them, he must compensate for them, without disagreement, because he received them without right. As for how he compensates for them, there are two well-known views mentioned by the author at the end of the chapter.

The sound view, which the majority affirmed and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, explicitly stated, is that he must pay their value.

The second view: he must pay their equivalent. These two views are based on whether fresh dates and grapes are fungible (mithli) or not. The sound and well-known view is that they are not fungible. If they dry up with the collector, then if they reach the amount of the zakat, it suffices; otherwise he returns the difference, or takes it. This is what the Iraqis and others said. Ibn Kajj related a view that it does not suffice in any case, because the act of taking possession is invalid. Al-Rafi'i said: this view is preferable, but the chosen view is what has preceded. End of al-Nawawi's words verbatim, and it is an explicit statement that fresh dates and grapes do not suffice, without disagreement among the Shafi'is.

Ibn al-Muhadhdhab's author said, and his exact words are: If he takes fresh dates, he must return them; if they are lost, he must return their value. Some of our companions said: he must return their equivalent, but the first view is the school's position, because they have no equivalent, since they vary, and for this reason it is not permitted to sell one part of them for another. End of quote verbatim, and it is an explicit statement that fresh dates do not suffice for the zakat on dates.

What we have mentioned from the majority of scholars, that zakat is taken only from dry dates and dry raisins, is the position of Malik and most of his companions. In the Muwatta' there is this text:

Malik said: The matter agreed upon among us is that palms are estimated for their owners while their fruit is still on the heads of the trees, once it has ripened and its sale is permitted, and its charity is taken from it as dates at the time of harvesting. He continued: The same practice applies to vineyards. End of the relevant part, verbatim. In it is Malik's clear statement, may Allah have mercy on him, that the matter agreed upon among the scholars of his time was that zakat is paid in dates. It clearly indicates that whoever claims that it is permitted to pay it from fresh dates or unripe dates, his claim contradicts the agreed matter according to Malik and the scholars of his time.

Among the clearest evidence for this is that unripe dates that do not become dates, and grapes that do not become raisins, like the unripe dates and grapes of Egypt, do not permit payment from them when the obligatory item, which is dry dates and dry raisins, cannot be obtained; rather, zakat is paid from their price or value according to Malik and his companions. They did not treat fresh dates and grapes as the origin, nor accept them as a substitute for the origin. They said: the price is obligatory if it is sold, and the value if it is eaten.

Khalil said in his Mukhtasar: "The price of what is not oil-bearing, and what does not dry." His meaning in saying "what does not dry" is that fresh dates and grapes that do not dry out must be paid from their price, not from the fresh dates and grapes themselves. In al-Mawwaq's commentary on Khalil's words, "and if it does not dry," his exact words are:

Malik said: If the fresh dates of this palm do not become dates, nor these grapes raisins, then it should be estimated as if that were possible; if the estimate is five awsuq, then it is taken from its price. End of the relevant part, verbatim. This is an explicit text from Malik that he does not consider paying zakat in fresh dates or grapes, since he turned from them to the price when dry dates and raisins cannot be obtained. How much more so in a situation where they can be obtained?

The conclusion is that paying fresh dates and grapes in place of dried ones is something no scholar has held, nor is it indicated by any evidence from the Qur'an, the Sunnah, or analogy. As for what does not dry, like the unripe dates and grapes of Egypt, there is a weak view among the Malikis permitting payment of fresh dates and grapes, and this view is related from Ibn Rushd. You will see, if Allah wills, at the end of this discussion, the statements of the Shafi'is and Hanbalis on it. If it is said: what is the evidence that only dry dates and dry raisins suffice, not fresh dates and grapes?

The answer: several pieces of evidence indicate this:

The first [proof] is the hadith we mentioned earlier, narrated by Attab ibn Asid (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that grapes be estimated (*kharṣ*) just as palm trees are estimated, and that their zakat be taken as raisins, just as the zakat of palm trees is taken as dates." We have already mentioned that this hadith was related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and al-Daraqutni. We have also mentioned that it is a *mursal* (a hadith in which the Companion is omitted from the chain, here narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib), and we mentioned that relying on this type of *mursal* from Sa'id is considered sound by the four Imams. So when you know the soundness of relying on this hadith of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, know that it is an explicit text stating: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that dates and grapes be estimated, and that the zakat on grapes be taken as raisins and the charity on palm trees be taken as dates." Whoever claims that it is permissible to take the zakat of palm trees as *rutab* (fresh dates) or *busr* (unripe dates) has a claim that contradicts what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered, because he ordered that it be taken in the state of being dates on the palm and raisins on the vine. It is well known that a state (*hal*) is a description of its bearer and a restriction on its agent. So the zakat of palm trees being dates is a description of it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that it be brought out in the state of being characterised by it. Likewise, its being dates is a restriction on its taking, so it is a restriction by the Prophet (ﷺ) on its taking, that it be in the state of being dates. It is understood from this that it is not to be taken in any other state, such as being *rutab*, for example. When it has become clear to you that taking it as *rutab*, for example, contradicts what he (ﷺ) ordered, know that he said in the hadith agreed upon (*muttafaq 'alayhi*): "Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something that is not part of it, it is rejected," and in a narration in the Sahih: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected." And in the Noble Book (Allah says): ﴿So let those who oppose his order beware﴾ [al-Nur: 63], and the verse continues.

What further clarifies to you that bringing out *rutab*, for example, as zakat contradicts what he (ﷺ) prescribed and legislated, namely taking it as dried dates and dried raisins, is what al-Bayhaqi mentioned in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*, in the chapter "How the zakat of palm trees and grapes is taken," where he said: "Abu al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Ma'ruf al-Faqih al-Mihrajani informed us, Bishr ibn Ahmad informed us, Ahmad ibn al-Husayn ibn Nasr al-Hadhdha' informed us, Ali ibn Abd Allah told us, Yazid ibn Zuray' told us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq told us, al-Zuhri informed me, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered Attab ibn Asid to estimate the grapes just as the palm trees are estimated, and then their zakat is to be paid as raisins, just as the zakat of palm trees is paid as dates." He said: "That is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning palm trees and grapes." End of quotation in its wording. In it is an explicit statement that bringing out dates and raisins is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the one who brings out *rutab* and grapes contradicts his Sunnah (ﷺ), as you see.

The second proof: the consensus of the Muslims that the zakat on fruits and grains is of the kind of thing whose very substance is subject to zakat, and the substance on which zakat is obligatory is dried dates and dried raisins, not *rutab* (p-517) or fresh grapes. This is supported by the consensus of those who hold the view of the *nisab* (minimum threshold) for fruits, that the five *awsuq* (sing. *wasq*), which constitute the *nisab*, are not counted from *rutab* or from grapes. So whoever has five *awsuq* of *rutab* or grapes, but when they dry they fall below five *awsuq*, there is no zakat on him, because the *nisab* is counted from dried dates and dried raisins. So if he brought out zakat from *rutab* or grapes, he would be bringing out from something other than that whose substance is subject to zakat, as you see. What supports this is what al-Zurqani mentioned in his *Sharh al-Muwatta'*, where he said in explaining Malik's words, "Then they pay the zakat on what has been estimated for them," the following text: "The basis of estimation (*takhrīṣ*) is to estimate what is in the palm trees or the grapes of dried dates when they are harvested, according to their kind, and what he knows of their state that it will become that at the time of drying (*itmār*), because the zakat is only taken from it as dates." End of the relevant passage in its wording.

It is established among the majority of scholars that the particle *innama* (only/indeed only) indicates restriction (*hasr*), and this is the truth. So al-Zurqani's words, "because the zakat is only taken from it as dates," mean: restricting the taking of the zakat of palm trees to dates specifically, excluding others such as *rutab* and the like, giving as the reason for counting the *nisab* from dried dates. Bringing out from that whose substance is subject to zakat among fruits and grains is clear. And what we have said is not refuted by the fact that the time when zakat becomes obligatory is the time of the fruit's ripening before it is dried, because the scholars agree that it is not obligatory to bring it out in practice until it becomes dried dates. They also agree that if a calamity (*jā'iḥa*) strikes it, it is taken into account, so the zakat of what was struck is dropped, just as the zakat of the whole is dropped if no *nisab* remains of it. Further clarification of this will come.

The third proof: that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to take it as dates after the harvesting (*jidhdh*), not as unripe dates, nor as *rutab*. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], and He says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and He says: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 80], and He says: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31], and other verses besides these.

Al-Bukhari said in his *Sahih*, in the chapter "Taking the charity of dates at the time of the palm harvest": "And does a child get left alone so that he touches the charity?" Umar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Asadi told us, my father told us, Ibrahim ibn Tahman told us, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to be brought dates at the time of the palm harvest. This one would come with his dates, and that one with his dates, until there was a heap of dates before him. Al-Hasan and al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them both) began playing with those dates, and one of them took a date and put it in his mouth. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at him and took it out of his mouth, and said: 'Do you not know that the family of Muhammad (ﷺ) do not eat charity?'" End of quotation.

This sound hadith is an explicit text that he (ﷺ) used to take the charity of palm trees as dates after the harvest. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence that the present tense form following the word *kāna* (was/used to), as in "he used to do such-and-such," indicates frequent repetition and constant persistence in that act. So Abu Hurayrah's words in this sound, attributed hadith, "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to be brought dates at the time of the palm harvest," (are decisive).

The hadith clearly indicates that bringing out dates at the harvest was what he (ﷺ) always did in his time, and that he took those dried dates in zakat. So whoever claims the permissibility of bringing out the zakat of palm trees as *rutab* or unripe dates (*balah*) contradicts what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was upon.

Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari*, in explaining the hadith mentioned just above, the following text: "Al-Isma'ili said: his words 'at the time of the palm harvest' mean after they have become dates, because palm trees may be harvested while still *rutab*, and then dried in the drying yard (*mirbad*), but this does not last long, so it is appropriate to attribute it to the harvest, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾, where the intention is after it has been threshed and cleaned. And Allah knows best." End of quotation in its wording, and it is clear regarding what we have mentioned.

From what we have mentioned, you know that what some later scholars claim, that it is permissible to bring out the zakat of palm trees as *rutab* and *busr*, is not correct, has no basis, and no evidence supports it. As for when the date fruit does not dry, such as the *balah* of Egypt, and its grapes, we have already mentioned from Malik and his companions that the zakat is taken from its price if it is sold, or from its value if it is eaten, not from the *rutab* or grapes themselves.

We have already mentioned from Ibn Rushd an opinion that is weaker (*marjuh*), permitting *rutab* and grapes specifically in the case of what does not dry. The position of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) regarding the zakat of what does not dry is: on the view that division (*qisma*) is a distinguishing of rights and not a sale, division is permitted, and a tenth or half of it is made distinct in certain palm trees; then the collector (*musaddiq*) considers: if he sees fit to distribute it to them, he does so; and if he sees fit to sell it and divide the price, he does so. But on the view that division is a sale, it is not permitted in *rutab* and grapes; the collector takes possession of its tenth as an undivided share by making it available between himself and it, and the ownership of the poor becomes fixed for them; then he sells it, takes its price, and distributes it among them. The same ruling applies in his view when there is need to cut the fruit as *rutab*, out of fear for it from thirst or the like.

The ruling on this question in the Hanbali school has two opinions:

The first: the official collector (*sa'i*) is given the choice between dividing the fruit with the owner of the property before harvesting by estimation (*kharṣ*), taking their share as a single palm tree and taking its fruit, or harvesting it and dividing it with him by measure, and distributing the fruit among the poor, or selling it to the owner of the property or to someone else, before or after harvesting, and distributing its price among the poor.

The second opinion: that the zakat on him is of dried dates and dried raisins. This was said by Abu Bakr, who mentioned that Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) explicitly stated it, as said by the author of *al-Mughni*. And what we have mentioned is the essence of Ahmad's school (may Allah have mercy on him) regarding the two issues: namely, fruit that does not dry, and fruit that needs to be cut before drying.

**Third issue:** Scholars differed over the time when zakat becomes obligatory on what the earth produces of fruit and grain. The majority of scholars said: for grain, it becomes obligatory when it hardens, and for fruit, when its ripeness appears. So the obligation is attached at the time the dates are ripe (ṭīb al-tamr), while the duty of paying it out comes after harvesting (al-jidhādh).

The benefit of this difference is that if a person disposes of the fruit or grain before the obligation arises, nothing is due from him; but if he disposes of it after zakat has become obligatory, the zakat is not dropped from him.

Another of its benefits: if he dies after the time of obligation, zakat is paid from his estate; if he dies before the obligation arises, zakat is paid from the estate of the heirs. Al-Qurtubi said in his commentary on this verse: Scholars differed about the time of obligation, in three opinions:

The first: it is the time of harvesting (al-jidhādh). This was said by Muhammad ibn Maslama, based on the words of God, Exalted: ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾.

The second: the day of ripeness (al-ṭayb), because what comes before ripeness is fodder, not staple food or provision. When it ripens and the eating that God has bestowed becomes available, the right that God commanded becomes due, since with the completion of the blessing the thanks for the blessing becomes obligatory, and the giving at the time of harvest is for what became due on the day of ripeness.

The third: it is after the estimation (al-kharṣ) is complete, because at that point the obligation of zakat in it is established, so it becomes a condition for its obligation, like the arrival of the collector (al-sāʿī) in the case of sheep. This was said by al-Mughira, and the correct view is the first, because of the explicit text of revelation, while the well-known view in the school is the second, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. End of his quote.

We have already mentioned that Malik, may God have mercy on him, says that everything the owner eats or gives in charity is counted against him, but the majority of scholars disagree with him on this. They argued that what he eats is not counted against him, by the words of God, Exalted: ﴿Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾. And by the hadith mentioned earlier: that the estimator should leave a third or a quarter.

The words of God, Exalted, ﴿on the day of its harvest﴾ were read by Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim with a fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, and the rest with a kasra, and both are well-known dialects, like al-ṣarrām and al-ṣirrām, al-jadhādh and al-jidhādh, al-qaṭāf and al-qiṭāf.

Benefit: When the owner of the orchard intends to harvest, it is fitting that he not prevent the poor from entering, and that he give them charity, by the words of God, Exalted, in condemning the people of the garden mentioned in Surah al-Qalam: ﴿When they swore that they would surely harvest it in the morning﴾ and the verses that follow [68:17]. And knowledge is with God, Exalted.

The words of God, Exalted: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, unless it be carrion, or flowing blood﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Anʿām: 145]. This noble verse explicitly states that nothing among foods has been forbidden except these four mentioned in it, namely: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God. But God, Exalted, has explained in some places the prohibition of things other than those mentioned, such as His explicit prohibition of wine in Surah al-Ma'ida by His words, Exalted: ﴿O you who believe! Intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are only an abomination of Satan's handiwork; so avoid it that you may prosper﴾.

Some scholars said: no food is forbidden except these four mentioned, and this is a view reported from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿĀʾisha. Al-Qurtubi said: the opposite of it is also reported from them. Al-Bukhari said in his Ṣaḥīḥ: ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, ʿAmr said: I said to Jabir ibn Zayd: "They claim that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys," and he said: "Ibn ʿAmr al-Ghifari used to say that ruling among us in Basra, but that the sea, Ibn ʿAbbas, refused it, and he recited: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾." End of quote. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad, from the Malikis, said: this verse includes the permissibility of every kind of animal and other things, except what is excepted in the verse: carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine.

For this reason we say: the flesh of predators and all other animals except humans and swine is permissible.

Al-Qurtubi said: It is narrated from ʿĀʾisha, Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn ʿUmar that eating the flesh of predators, donkeys, and mules is permissible, and he mentioned the hadith of al-Bukhari that we have just cited.

Then he said: It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he was asked about the flesh of predators, and he said: "There is no harm in it." It was said to him: "The hadith of Abu Thaʿlaba al-Khushani." He said: "We do not leave the Book of our Lord for the hadith of a Bedouin who urinates on his shins."

Al-Shaʿbi was asked about the flesh of the elephant and the lion, and he recited this verse.

Al-Qasim said: ʿĀʾisha used to say, when she heard people saying "every fanged predator is forbidden": that is lawful, and she would recite this verse: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me﴾ to the end of the verse.

(p-521) Its author, may God forgive him, said: Know that in this discussion we intend to explain the proof of those who say that the flesh of predators, donkeys, and the like is not forbidden, and the proof of those who say it is forbidden, then mention the stronger view with its evidence.

Know first: the claim that no food other than the four mentioned in this verse is forbidden is false, by the consensus of Muslims, by the consensus of all Muslims, and by the indication of the Book and the Sunna on the prohibition of wine. So it is a decisive proof of the prohibition of things other than the four.

Whoever claims that wine is lawful by this verse is a disbeliever, without dispute among scholars. Knowing this, know that those who used this verse as evidence that what was mentioned is not forbidden said: God restricted the prohibited things in it to the four mentioned, and He also restricted them in Surah al-Nahl in His words: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God﴾ [al-Baqara: 173]; because innama is a particle of restriction according to the majority, and al-Nahl comes after al-Anʿam, as shown by His words in al-Nahl: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you before﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nahl: 118], and what is related and referred to is what is mentioned in al-Anʿam, in His words: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Anʿam: 146]; and because He, Exalted, said in al-Anʿam: ﴿Those who associated partners will say: Had God willed, we would not have associated﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Anʿam: 148], then He stated in al-Nahl that they actually said that, in His words: ﴿And those who associated said: Had God willed, we would not have worshipped besides Him anything﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Nahl: 135]. This shows that al-Nahl comes after al-Anʿam. He also restricted the prohibition to the four mentioned in Surah al-Baqara, in His words: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God﴾. They said: this heavenly restriction, which the angel brought repeatedly, in Mecca in al-Anʿam and al-Nahl, and in Medina at the legislation of rulings in al-Baqara, cannot be opposed by us, nor can anything be removed from it except by a proof that is definitive in its text, mutawatir like the mutawatir transmission of the Great Qur'an.

So wine, for example, the Qur'an indicates is prohibited, so we prohibit it, because its proof is definitive. As for others such as predators, donkeys, and mules: the proofs of their prohibition are single reports (akhbar ahad), which are overridden by the definitive text, namely the verses mentioned above.

* *

Note

Know that what al-Qurtubi and others mentioned, that the addition by the Sunna of the prohibition of predators and donkeys, for example, to the four mentioned in the verses, is like the addition by the Sunna of exile (taghrib) to the hundred lashes for the fornicator, established by the Qur'an, or the addition of judgment by one witness and an oath in property matters, established by the Sunna, to the two witnesses, or the witness and two women mentioned in His words: ﴿But if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾ [al-Baqara: 282], is not clearly valid in my view; because the difference between the two matters is clear. The addition of exile and of judgment by one witness and an oath to the verse: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each of them﴾ [al-Nur: 2], in the first case, and to the verse: ﴿But if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾, in the second case, is an addition of something the Qur'an did not address with either negation or affirmation, and such an addition is not prohibited according to the majority of scholars, because addition to the text is not abrogation of it according to the majority, unlike Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him.

Based on that, he prohibited exile and judgment by one witness and an oath, because addition, in his view, is abrogation, and the Qur'an is not abrogated by single reports, since it is definitive in its text, and these are not. But the addition of another prohibited thing to His words: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me﴾ to the end of the verse is not an addition of something the Qur'an was silent about, like the first case; rather it is an addition of something the Qur'an negated, because the Qur'anic restriction indicates the negation of prohibition regarding anything other than the four mentioned. The difference between the two matters is clear. By this you know that Malik, may God have mercy on him, is not among those who say that addition to the text is abrogation, except when the addition establishes what had been negated by the text before it; then its being abrogating is clear. There is another consideration, said by some scholars: that the permissibility of things other than the four mentioned is rational permissibility, known to the jurists as original exemption (al-barā'a al-aṣliyya), which is the presumption of original non-existence, since the original position is that nothing is prohibited except by proof, as stated by a group of jurists.

If its permissibility is rational, then lifting it is not abrogation, so that the abrogating text would need to be mutawatir. Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir attributed this view, that there is no abrogation, to the majority of later scholars.

Its author, may God forgive him, said: That it is abrogation seems more evident to me; because the restriction in the verse conveys that everything other than the four is permitted by the law, so it is legal permissibility, indicated by the Qur'an; and lifting a legal permissibility is abrogation without dispute. In Marāqī al-Suʿūd he indicated that an addition that does not contradict the first ruling is not abrogation, saying:

*Not every addition is abrogation,*
*in what is established by the text as an increase.*

This is the view of the majority of scholars, and they argued that addition does not contradict what is added to, and what does not contradict cannot be abrogating, and this is clear.

Know that Malik ibn Anas, may God have mercy on him, had differing reports on the flesh of predators. It is reported from him that it is forbidden, and this is the view he confined himself to in the Muwatta', since he titled a section on the prohibition of eating every fanged predator, then transmitted with his chain the hadith of Abu Thaʿlaba al-Khushani, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): that he forbade eating every fanged predator; then he transmitted with his chain the hadith of Abu Hurayra, raised to the Prophet: "Eating every fanged predator is forbidden," then he said: "And this is the practice among us." This is explicit that the sound view in his school is its prohibition, and al-Qurtubi affirmed that this is the sound view of his school. It is also reported from him that they are disliked (makruh), and this is the apparent view of the Mudawwana, and the well-known view among his school. The evidence for this view is the verses we mentioned, among them the verse we are concerned with.

What is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, and ʿĀʾisha of their permissibility is the view of al-Awza'i.

Its author, may God forgive him, said: What appears to be stronger by evidence is what the majority held: that everything whose prohibition is established by a sound channel from the Book or the Sunna is forbidden, and is added to the four mentioned in the verses, and there is no contradiction in that with the Qur'an, because the prohibited things added to them were prohibited after them.

The scholars have established that no contradiction arises between two propositions when their times differ, since it is possible that each is true at its own time. Most of the theologians (al-nuzzar) stipulated for contradiction that the time be the same, because if it differs, both can be true at their respective times. For example, if you say, "The Bayt al-Maqdis was not faced (in prayer)," and "The Bayt al-Maqdis was faced," and you mean by the first what came after the abrogation (naskh, the lifting of a earlier ruling by a later one) and by the second what came before it, then both are true.

I have indicated in my versified work on logic (fann al-mantiq) that for two propositions to be contradictory they must be identical in every respect other than quality, meaning affirmation and negation, in terms of time, place, condition, relation, potentiality, action, actualization, privation, subject, predicate, part and whole. I stated this in my verse:

*"Identity is necessary between the two in all respects except quality, such as condition, known,*
*and part and whole, together with place, action, potentiality and time,*
*relation, actualization or privation, and unity of subject and predicate."*

At the time of the revelation of the verses mentioned, nothing was forbidden apart from the four mentioned. Therefore the restriction (hasr) stated then was true before anything else was forbidden, without any doubt. When the prohibition of something else arises through a new cause, this does not contradict the earlier restriction, because it occurred after it. This is the verified position, God willing. From it becomes clear that the correct view is that a mutawatir (widely transmitted) text may be abrogated by an authentic sunnah (prophetic practice) whose lateness relative to it is established, although most of the scholars of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) have prohibited this.

Having understood this, we will now, God willing, detail the things prohibited after this, and the opinions of the scholars concerning them.

Among them is every carnivorous animal with fangs (dhu nab min al-sibaa'). The verified position is that it is forbidden, on the basis of what we have already cited from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani concerning the prohibition of them and their being forbidden. As for the hadith of Abu Tha'labah, it is agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). As for the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, Muslim transmitted it in his Sahih from him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with the wording: "Every fanged carnivore, its eating is forbidden."

The hadiths on this subject are numerous, and by this you know that the verified position is the prohibition of eating every fanged carnivore.

The verified position is also that eating every bird of prey with talons (dhu mikhlab min al-tayr) is prohibited. No weight is given to the view of those among the Malikis and others who said that the prohibition from him (ﷺ) was not established, because it is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that he (ﷺ) "forbade every fanged carnivore and every bird of prey with talons." End of quote.

In the Sahih he combined it with what explicitly states it is forbidden, even though each of them is possessed of hostility and predation. All of this shows that it is prohibited.

The default meaning of a prohibition is haram (forbidden). By the prohibition of the fanged carnivore and the bird of prey with talons, the majority of scholars, including the three Imams (Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad) and Dawud (al-Zahiri), held the view.

We have already mentioned that the correct position from Malik regarding carnivores is the one that is authentically reported, and that the well-known position of his school is reprehensibility (karahah). From him there is also an opinion permitting them, which is the weakest of them. The correct view is prohibition, for the reasons we have stated.

Among these is the domestic donkey (al-humur al-ahliyyah). The verified position here too is that it is forbidden, and no fair-minded person should doubt its prohibition, because of the abundance of authentic hadiths that have come concerning its prohibition. Al-Bukhari and Muslim have both related its prohibition from the hadiths of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Salamah ibn al-Akwa', 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, Anas, and Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may Allah be pleased with them all. Their hadiths clearly indicate prohibition. The wording of the hadith of Abu Tha'labah in al-Bukhari and Muslim is: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys," which is wholly explicit in prohibition. The wording of the hadith of Anas in both of them is also: "Indeed Allah and His Messenger forbid you the flesh of domestic donkeys, for it is impure (rijs)." In a narration of Muslim: "for it is impure (rijs) of the work of Satan." In another narration of his: "for it is rijs" or "najas" (filth).

The author of these notes (qayyiduhu), may Allah pardon him, says: This hadith of Anas, which is agreed upon, in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) declared that the flesh of domestic donkeys is rijs, is explicit in the prohibition of eating it and in the impurity (najasah) of its flesh. The reason for its prohibition is not that its khums (fifth share) was not taken out, nor that it is a beast of burden (hamulah), as some scholars have claimed. And Allah knows best.

These authentic hadiths, agreed upon, are not contradicted by what Abu Dawud related from the hadith of Ghalib ibn Abjar al-Muzani, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, drought has struck us, and I had nothing in my wealth to feed my family except fat donkeys, and you have forbidden domestic donkeys.' He said: 'Feed your family from the fat of your donkeys, for I only forbade them because of the jawwal of the town.'" End of quote.

Al-jawwal is the plural of jallalah, which is the animal that eats jallah, and jallah is originally dung. What is meant here is the eating of impurities such as filth.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: The huffaz (memorizers of hadith) agreed on the weakness of this hadith.

Al-Khattabi and al-Bayhaqi said: It is a hadith whose isnad (chain) is disputed, meaning it is mudtarib (inconsistent in transmission). Whatever is like this is not used to contradict hadiths that are agreed upon.

As for mules, their eating is also not permissible, because of what Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade, on the day of Khaybar, the flesh of domestic donkeys, the flesh of mules, every fanged carnivore, and every bird of prey with talons." The origin of this hadith of Jabir is in the two Sahihs as already mentioned, and it is with this wording, with a chain that is not objectionable. Ibn Hajar and al-Shawkani said this.

Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir: Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud related with two chains, each of them on the condition of Muslim, from Jabir who said: "On the day of Khaybar we slaughtered horses, mules and donkeys, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade us from mules and donkeys, and did not forbid us from horses." This is clear evidence for the prohibition of mules. It is supported by the fact that they are born of donkeys, which are definitely forbidden, due to the soundness of the texts prohibiting them.

* *

As for horses, the scholars have differed regarding the permissibility of eating them:

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, prohibited them in one of the two opinions attributed to him, and from him there is also the view that they are reprehensible (makruh). Each of the two opinions was declared sound by some Malikis, and prohibition is the more well-known among them.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I dislike the flesh of horses." Abu Bakr al-Razi interpreted this as tanzih (reprehension short of prohibition), and said: "Abu Hanifah did not use the word prohibition for them, and they are not in his view like the domestic donkey."

The author of al-Muhit, the author of al-Hidayah, and the author of al-Dhakhirah declared the prohibition to be the view attributed to him, and this is the opinion of most of the Hanafis.

Among those from whom I have related the reprehensibility of eating horse flesh are: al-Awza'i, Abu 'Ubayd, Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hakam.

The position of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, may they both be blessed by Allah, is the permissibility of eating horses, and this is the view of most of the people of knowledge.

Among those who said it is permissible: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd, Anas ibn Malik, Asma' bint Abi Bakr, Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, 'Alqamah, al-Aswad, 'Ata', Shurayh, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Ishaq, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Dawud, and others.

This is as al-Nawawi transmitted from them in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab. We will, God willing, clarify the proofs of all of them, and which view the evidence indicates is preponderant.

Know that whoever prohibited eating horse flesh based his argument on a verse and a hadith.

As for the verse, it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride and for adornment﴾ [al-Nahl: 8]. He said: The Exalted has said: ﴿And the cattle He created for you, in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ [al-Nahl: 5]. So these are for eating. And He said: ﴿And the horses, mules and donkeys, for you to ride,﴾ so these are for riding, not for eating. This is a detailing by the One who created them and bestowed favour through them. He emphasized this by several matters:

First: the lam (of purpose) indicates causation, meaning He created them for you for the cause of riding and adornment, because a stated cause implies restriction (hasr). Thus the permission to eat them contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse.

Second: He joined mules and donkeys to them, which indicates that they share with them in the ruling of prohibition.

Third: the noble verse was given in the context of favour, and Surat al-Nahl is called the Surah of Favours.

A wise One does not bestow favour with the lowest of blessings while leaving the highest, especially since favour was bestowed by means of eating in the things mentioned before them.

Fourth: if eating them were permitted, the benefit of them in what favour was bestowed upon, namely riding and adornment, would be lost.

As for the hadith, it is what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys."

The majority rejected the use of the noble verse as evidence, on the grounds that the verse of al-Nahl was revealed in Makkah by consensus, while the permission to eat horses on the day of Khaybar came more than six years after the Hijrah from Makkah. Had the Prophet (ﷺ) understood a prohibition from the verse, he would not have permitted eating. Also, the verse of al-Nahl is not explicit in prohibiting the eating of horses; rather, the prohibition was understood from the stated cause and from the hadith of Jabir and the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, both agreed upon. Both are explicit in the permissibility of eating horses, and the explicit statement (manțuq) takes precedence over the implied meaning (mafhum), as is established in usul al-fiqh.

Also, even if we grant the validity of the indicated proof of the verse, it only indicates leaving off eating, and leaving off is more general than being prohibited, or being reprehensible, or being contrary to the better course. When none of these is specified, the reliance on the proofs that explicitly state permissibility remains.

Also, even if we grant that the lam indicates causation, we do not grant that it implies restriction to riding and adornment. Horses are useful for other things besides these, and for other things besides eating by consensus. He only mentioned riding and adornment because they are the most common purposes for which horses are sought.

A parallel to this is the hadith of the cow mentioned in the two Sahihs, when she addressed her rider and said: "We were not created for this; we were created for ploughing." Even though it is more explicit in restriction, it intended only the most common purpose. Otherwise, the cow is eaten and benefited from in things other than ploughing, by consensus.

Also, even if the mentioned inference were granted, it would necessitate prohibiting the carrying of loads on horses, mules and donkeys, on account of the alleged restriction to riding and adornment, and no one holds this.

As for the inference from the conjoining of donkeys and mules to them, it is an inference by the indication of juxtaposition (dalalat al-iqtiran). Most scholars of usul have weakened it, as indicated in Maraqi al-Su'ud in his verse:

*"As for the juxtaposition of wording in the well-known [usage], it does not equate except in what is mentioned."*

As for the inference that the noble verse was given in the context of favour, it is answered by saying that it intended what benefit from it was most common among the Arabs, so they were addressed with what they knew and were accustomed to. They were not accustomed to eating horses because of their scarcity in their lands and their great need for them in fighting. By contrast, most of their benefit from cattle was for carrying loads and for eating. So in each of the two categories favour was mentioned with the most common benefit from it.

If restriction followed from this in this part, the same would follow in the other part, as we have stated.

As for the inference that permitting their eating is a cause of their extinction and disappearance, it is answered by saying: He permitted the eating of cattle, and they did not become extinct. Even if fear of that were a cause for prohibition in cattle, so that they would not become extinct and their benefit in things other than eating would be lost. Ibn Hajar said this.

As for the inference from the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, it is rejected on two grounds:

The first: the scholars of hadith have weakened it. Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari under the chapter "The Flesh of Horses," the following text: "The hadith of Khalid has been weakened by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Musa ibn Harun, al-Daraqutni, al-Khattabi, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, 'Abd al-Haqq, and others."

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: The scholars of hadith and others agreed that the hadith of Khalid mentioned above is weak. He mentioned the chains of some of them to that effect. The hadith of Khalid, in addition to being *mudtarib* (irregular in its transmission), has in its chain Salih ibn Yahya ibn al-Miqdam ibn Ma'di Karib, whom more than one scholar declared weak. Ibn Hajar said of him in *al-Taqrib*: "layyin" (lenient, i.e., weak in narration). Also in its chain is his father Yahya, the one who is his teacher in this hadith, of whom Ibn Hajar said in *al-Taqrib*: "mastur" (unknown in reliability).

The second point: even if we grant that the hadith of Khalid is not weak, it is opposed by what is stronger than it, such as the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ forbade the eating of donkey meat on the day of Khaybar, and permitted the eating of horse meat." In a wording in the *Sahih*: "and he allowed the eating of horse meat." Also the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "We slaughtered a horse during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and we ate it," agreed upon by both (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

There is no doubt that these two are stronger than the hadith of Khalid. From all of this you know that the explicit evidence points to the preponderance of the permissibility of eating horse meat, and Allah knows best. It is not hidden that leaving the disagreement is more cautious, as some scholars said:

[Rajaz]
Indeed, the most scrupulous one is he who exits their disagreement, even if the (view) is weak, so discern.

Among these is the dog: eating it is forbidden according to the general body of scholars, and there is a very weak opinion from Malik that it is merely disliked.

There are many proofs for its prohibition. Among them is what has preceded regarding beasts of prey with fangs, since the dog is a beast of prey with fangs. Among them also: if its eating were permissible, its sale would be permissible, and the prohibition of its price has been established in the *Sahihayn* from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, coupled with the payment of the soothsayer and the wages of the prostitute. Al-Bukhari narrated it from the hadith of Abu Juhayfa, and Muslim narrated it from the hadith of Rafi' ibn Khadij, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "The price of the dog is evil," and so on. That is an explicit text on prohibition, due to His saying: ﴿And he makes unlawful for them the evil things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

If it is said: not every evil thing is prohibited, because the garlic was described as evil, and the earnings of the cupper were described as evil, yet neither of them is prohibited.

The answer: what has been established by explicit text as evil, that is evidence for its prohibition, and what is excluded by evidence is excluded, and the text remains a proof regarding what no evidence has come to exclude. This is the ruling in most of the general statements of the Qur'an and Sunnah: some individual cases are excluded by a specifier, and the rest remain a proof. This is the view of the majority, and in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* he alluded to it with his words:

[Rajaz]
It is a proof according to most, if a specifier making it clear is specified.

If it is said: the prohibition of the evil things is due to the effective cause of evil, and if an evil thing is found that is not prohibited, that would be a breaking of the cause (naqd fi al-'illa), not a specification of it.

The answer: most scholars hold that a breaking (naqd) is a specification of the cause, not its invalidation. In *Maraqi al-Su'ud* he said:

[Rajaz]
Among them: the presence of the attribute without the ruling, which the transmitters of knowledge named "breaking" (naqd), and most of them do not consider it harmful; rather it is a specification, and this is the sound position.

Etc. ... as we have verified in a place other than this.

Among the proofs for the prohibition of the dog: what is established in the *Sahihayn* of explicit hadiths on the prohibition of keeping it, and that keeping it reduces the reward of its keeper every day. So if its eating were permissible, its keeping would be permissible.

The Prophet ﷺ permitted only the hunting dog, the farm dog, and the livestock dog, out of necessity. Among the evidence for this: what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever keeps a dog, other than a hunting dog, a farm dog, or a livestock dog, his reward is reduced by a qirat every day." Also from it: what the two Shaykhs narrated in their *Sahihayn* from the hadith of Sufyan ibn Abi Zuhayr al-Shana'i, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever keeps a dog that does not benefit him with crops or livestock, his deeds are reduced by a qirat every day." Al-Bukhari narrated it from Ibn Umar by three routes with the wording: "his deeds are reduced every day by two qirats," and Muslim also narrated it from Ibn Umar through several routes, in some of which it is one qirat and in some two qirats.

The hadiths on this subject are many. This is the clearest proof that the dog is not lawful to eat, for if its eating were lawful, its keeping for eating would be lawful, and this is evident. Among them also: what is established in *Sahih Muslim* from the hadith of Jabir, Abd Allah ibn Umar, and Abd Allah ibn al-Mughaffal, may Allah be pleased with them, that the Prophet ﷺ ordered the killing of dogs. Had it been lawful to eat, he would not have ordered its killing, and he did not permit them except for the necessity of hunting, farming, or livestock.

When you know that in the hunting dog, and what is mentioned with it, there are some permissible benefits, such as benefiting from its hunt, or its guarding of livestock or crops, know that the scholars differed regarding its sale.

Some of them said: its sale follows its meat, and its meat is prohibited, so its sale is prohibited. This is the strongest of the opinions in terms of evidence, because of what we have mentioned: that the price of the dog is evil, and that the Prophet ﷺ forbade it, coupled with the payment of the soothsayer and the wages of the prostitute. This is a sound, explicit text prohibiting its sale.

This is supported by what Abu Dawud narrated with a sound chain from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, traced to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the price of the dog," and said: "If one comes seeking the price of a dog, fill his palm with dust."

Al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, and Ibn Hajar in *al-Fath*, said: its chain is sound. Abu Dawud also narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "The price of the dog is not lawful, nor the payment of the soothsayer, nor the wages of the prostitute." Ibn Hajar said in *al-Fath*: its chain is good (hasan). Al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* said: its chain is good and sound.

When you have verified that, know that the view of prohibiting the sale of the dog, which we have mentioned as the truth, is general, covering both the dog whose keeping is permitted and others, because of the generality of the evidences. Among those who held this view: Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, Rabi'a, al-Hakam, Hammad, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others. It is also the well-known sound position of the school of Malik, contrary to what al-Qurtubi mentioned in *al-Mufhim*, that the well-known position of his school is disapproval. It is also narrated from Malik the permissibility of selling the hunting dog and the like, but not the one whose keeping is not permitted, and this is the view of Sahnun, for he said: "I sell the hunting dog and perform Hajj with its price."

Abu Hanifa permitted its sale absolutely if there is some benefit in it, such as hunting or guarding livestock, for example. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted something similar from Jabir, Ata', and al-Nakha'i, as al-Nawawi said.

If a dog whose keeping is permitted, such as the hunting dog, is killed, then there is its value (qimah) according to Malik; there is nothing due for it according to Ahmad and al-Shafi'i; and Abu Hanifa made the value obligatory for it absolutely if it has some benefit.

The argument of those who say there is no value due is that the value is a price, and the sound text forbade the price of the dog, and there came the explicit statement that whoever seeks it, his palm is filled with dust, and that is the most emphatic expression of prohibiting it.

Those who made the value obligatory argued that he destroyed a lawful benefit, so he owes compensation for it.

Those who permitted selling the dog and required its value if killed argued with what is narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ "forbade the price of the dog except the hunting dog," and from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he made a man pay twenty camels for a dog he had killed, and from Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As that he ruled regarding a hunting dog killed by a man at forty dirhams, and he ruled regarding a livestock dog at a ram.

They also argued that a dog whose keeping is permitted may be bequeathed and benefited from, so it is like the donkey.

The majority answered that the hadiths and reports narrated regarding the permissibility of selling the hunting dog and the obligation of its value are all weak.

Al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* said, in its exact words: "As for the answer to what they argued with from the hadiths and reports, all of them are weak by the agreement of the hadith scholars." Likewise, al-Tirmidhi, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi made clear their weakness. The argument from the permissibility of bequeathing it and its likeness to the donkey is rejected by the sound explicit texts stating that its price is not lawful. As for what Ibn Asim al-Maliki said in his *Tuhfa*:

[Rajaz]
They agreed that the dogs of the desert may be sold, like the dog of the livestock.

Then the scholars of the Maliki school refuted him, may Allah have mercy on him, and we have already mentioned that this is the view of Sahnun.

Know that what is narrated from Jabir and Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet ﷺ, indicating the permissibility of selling the hunting dog, is all weak, as Ibn Hajar explained its weakness in *Fath al-Bari* in the chapter "The Price of the Dog."

Al-Qurtubi said: Some people claimed that among the Arabs none ate dog meat except a people of Faq'as.

* *

Among these is the monkey, for it is not lawful to eat. Al-Qurtubi said in his *Tafsir*: Abu Umar, meaning Ibn Abd al-Barr, said: The Muslims agreed that it is not lawful to eat the monkey, due to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbidding its eating, and it is not lawful to sell it, since it has no benefit.

He said: I do not know of anyone who permitted its eating except what Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, from Ayyub: Mujahid was asked about eating the monkey, and he said: "It is not of the cattle (bahimat al-an'am)." I say: Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned that he said: We have it narrated from Ata' that he was asked about a monkey killed in the Sacred Precinct, and he said: "Two just men shall judge it." He said: According to the school of Ata', eating its meat is permissible, since the penalty is not obligatory on one who kills other than game. And in *Bahr al-Madhhab* by al-Ruyani, according to the school of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Shafi'i said: The sale of the monkey is permissible, since it can be trained and benefited from for guarding goods. End.

Al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* said: The monkey is forbidden according to us, and this is the view of Ata', Ikrima, Mujahid, Makhul, al-Hasan, and Ibn Habib of the Maliki school.

Ibn Qudama said in *al-Mughni*: Ibn Abd al-Barr said: I know of no disagreement among the scholars of the Muslims that the monkey is not eaten and its sale is not lawful. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that the Prophet ﷺ "forbade the meat of the monkey," and because it is a beast of prey, it falls under the generality of the report, and because it is also a transformed creature (maskh), so it is among the forbidden evil things.

We have already mentioned the firm verdict of Ibn Habib and Ibn Abd al-Barr from the Malikis that it is forbidden. Al-Baji said: "In my view, the more evident position of Malik and his companions is that it is not forbidden."

Among these is the elephant. The apparent view regarding it is that it is among the beasts of prey with fangs, and we have already mentioned that the verified ruling regarding them is prohibition, due to its authenticity from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this is the view of the majority.

Among those who authenticated it from the Malikis: Ibn Abd al-Barr and al-Qurtubi.

Some of the Malikis said its disapproval is lighter than the disapproval of a beast of prey. Ashhab permitted it. And it is narrated from Malik in *al-Mudawwana* the disapproval of benefiting from ivory, which is the tusk of the elephant.

Ibn Qudama said in *al-Mughni*: The elephant is forbidden. Ahmad said: It is not among the foods of the Muslims. al-Hasan said: It is a transformed creature. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i disapproved of it, and al-Sha'bi permitted eating it. Our proof is the Prophet ﷺ's prohibition of eating every beast of prey with fangs, and it is among the greatest in fangs; and because it is regarded as repugnant, it falls under the generality of the verse prohibiting the evil things. End.

Al-Nawawi in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* said: The elephant is forbidden according to us, and according to Abu Hanifa and the Kufans, and al-Hasan. al-Sha'bi, Ibn Shihab, and Malik in one narration permitted it.

The proof of the first group is that it has fangs. End.

Among these are the house cat, the fox, and the bear: according to Malik they are among the beasts of prey with fangs. In another narration from him, they are disliked as a matter of abstention (karahat tanzih), with no prohibition in them according to one view. The domestic and wild cat are the same according to him.

al-Shinqiti, Adwa' al-Bayan, commentary on Surah 6, verse 145 (part 4 of 6):

Other imams, such as al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Abu Hanifa, differentiated between them, so they forbade the domestic (animal).

Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: As for the domestic (animal), it is forbidden according to the view of our imam, Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i.

It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he «forbade eating the cat». Ibn Qudamah also said in al-Mughni: The narrations differed concerning the fox. Most of the narrations from Ahmad state that it is forbidden, and this is the view of Abu Hurayrah, Malik and Abu Hanifa, because it is a predator (sabu'), so it falls under the general scope of the prohibition. It was narrated from Ahmad that it is permissible, and this was chosen by al-Sharif Abu Ja'far. 'Ata', Tawus, Qatadah, al-Laith, Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and al-Shafi'i permitted it, because it is ransomed (in expiation) when one is in ihram and in the Haram. He went on to say: The narrations from Ahmad differed concerning the wild cat (sinnawr al-barr), and the ruling on it is the same as the ruling on the fox.

al-Nawawi related the consensus of the Shafi'is on the permissibility of the fox. The author of al-Muhadhdhab said: Regarding the wild cat (sinnawr al-wahsh) there are two opinions:
The first: it is not lawful, because it hunts with its fang, so it is not lawful, like the lion and the leopard.
The second: it is lawful, because it is an animal that divides into a wild kind and a domestic kind, so the domestic kind is forbidden and the wild kind is lawful, like the donkey.

As for the bear (al-dubb): it is a predator with fangs according to Malik, al-Shafi'i and the companions of Abu Hanifa. Ahmad said: If the bear has fangs, its eating is prohibited; if it has no fangs, there is no harm in eating it.

The scholars differed regarding the permissibility of eating the hyena (al-dab'): according to Malik it is like the fox, and we have previously cited that from him that it is a predator in one narration, while in another it is disliked, and there is no statement of prohibition regarding it. The hadiths we previously cited in Surah al-Ma'idah, that the hyena is game (sayd), indicate the permissibility of eating it. It was narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas that he used to eat hyenas; this was related by al-Qurtubi. al-Shafi'i and others permitted eating it. al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra: al-Shafi'i said: The meat of hyenas is only sold in Makkah between al-Safa and al-Marwah.

The argument of Malik in his well-known school: the hyena is among the predators, so it falls under the general scope of the prohibition on eating every fanged predator, and he did not single out one predator from another. al-Qurtubi said: The hadith of the hyena which al-Nasa'i narrated concerning its permissibility is not something that can be set against the hadith of prohibition, because it is a hadith transmitted solely by Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi 'Ammar, who is not well known for transmitting knowledge, and is not one whose report is used as evidence when it contradicts one more reliable than him. Abu 'Umar said: The prohibition of eating every fanged predator has been narrated through mutawatir chains; a group of trustworthy and reliable imams related it, and it is impossible that they would be contradicted by something like the hadith of Ibn Abi 'Ammar. End of quote.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: The opponent may say that the hadiths of prohibition are general concerning every fanged predator, while the evidence for the permissibility of the hyena is specific, and a general and a specific do not conflict, because the specific takes precedence over the general, so its generality is specified by it, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence.

Among these is the hedgehog (al-qunfudh). Some scholars held that it is forbidden; this is the view of Imam Ahmad and Abu Hurayrah. The majority, among them Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Laith, Abu Thawr and others, permitted eating it.

Those who forbade it relied on what Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Hurayrah that he said: «The hedgehog was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "It is one of the filthy things (khaba'ith)."»

Those who permitted it, who are the majority, argued that the hadith is not established, and that there is no prohibition except with evidence. al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra, after citing the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned above concerning the filthiness of the hedgehog: This is a hadith that was not narrated except through this chain, and it is a chain with weakness in it.

Among those who disliked eating the hedgehog: Abu Hanifa and his companions. al-Qurtubi and others said this.

* *

Among these are the insects of the earth: such as the mouse, snakes, vipers, scorpions, the khunfusa beetle, the lizard (al-'azayah), frogs, rats (al-jirdhan), the gecko (al-wazagh), cockroaches, spiders, the wall-lizard (sam abras), dung beetles (al-ji'lan), the bina't wardan, worms (al-didan), the weevil (himar qabban), and similar things.

The majority of scholars hold the eating of these things to be forbidden, because they are naturally regarded as repugnant, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And He makes unlawful for them the filthy things﴾.

Among those who said this: al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, Ibn Shihab, 'Urwah and others, may Allah have mercy on them all.

Malik permitted eating them, but stipulated for the permissibility of eating snakes that their venom be safe.

Among those narrated as permitting the eating of insects: al-Awza'i and Ibn Abi Layla. They relied on what Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from the hadith of Milqam ibn Talib, from his father Talib ibn Tha'labah ibn Rabi'ah al-Tamimi al-'Anbari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I accompanied the Prophet ﷺ and I never heard a prohibition regarding the insects of the earth.

They also argued that Allah prohibited some things and permitted some things; what He prohibited is forbidden, what He permitted is permissible, and what He was silent about is pardoned.

'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said about the mouse: It is not forbidden, and she recited His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾, the verse.

This is answered by: Milqam ibn Talib is obscure (mastur), his condition is not known; and the statement of his father Talib ibn Tha'labah, may Allah be pleased with him, "I never heard a prohibition regarding the insects of the earth," does not indicate the absence of their prohibition, as al-Khattabi and al-Bayhaqi said, because a companion not hearing something does not necessitate its non-existence, as is well known. And also: Allah did not remain silent about this, because He prohibited the filthy things, and these are filthy things which no sound nature can readily accept, let alone find pleasant. Those among the Arabs who eat such insects are driven to it only by severe hunger, as one of their poets said:

[Al-Tawil]
"We have eaten the field mice, O Umm 'Amr, and whoever is a stranger among you eats insects."

Al-Ruba is the plural of ruba, which is the mouse, as al-Qurtubi said; in al-Lisan it is a small creature between the mouse and Umm Hubayn. Because of that severe need, when some Arabs were asked what they eat, he said: Everything that crawls and walks, except Umm Hubayn. So he said: May Umm Hubayn be granted well-being.

It is established in sound hadiths that the Prophet ﷺ permitted killing the mouse and what is mentioned with it of the vermin (fawasiq), which indicates that it is not permissible to eat them.

Know that what some scholars, such as al-Shafi'i, mentioned, that everything which a sound nature of the Arabs, to whom the Qur'an was revealed, finds repugnant, outside a state of dire hunger, is forbidden, based on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He makes unlawful for them the filthy things﴾, the verse, is a clear inference; there is no basis for the rejection by the Zahiris that this is a matter on which a ruling cannot be founded because it is not definable; for the meaning of filthiness (khubth) is known to them, so whatever is characterised by it is forbidden, by the verse.

This is not undermined by the explicit permission of some repugnant things, such as garlic, because what the evidence has excluded is specified from the general text, and it remains binding in what evidence has not excluded, as we have previously stated.

Also included is everything which the Shari'ah explicitly states to be filthy (khabith), unless there is evidence indicating its permissibility, together with the application of the name khubth to it.

Some scholars excepted from the insects of the earth the gecko (al-wazagh). Some of them claimed consensus on its prohibition, as Ibn Qudamah mentioned in al-Mughni from Ibn 'Abd al-Barr.

The author of this commentary (may Allah pardon him) says: What supports this is the hadith of Umm Sharik, agreed upon, that he ﷺ commanded the killing of geckos. Likewise, al-Shaykhan also narrated it from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, connected (mawsul) in Muslim, and possibly mursal in al-Bukhari, for his saying: "Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas claimed that he commanded its killing" may be from the statement of 'A'ishah, or it may be from the statement of 'Urwah; in either case the hadith is connected. It is possible that it is from the statement of al-Zuhri, in which case it is disconnected (munqati'). Ibn Hajar preferred this in al-Fath, and said: It seems al-Zuhri connected it for Ma'mar and sent it for Yunus. End of quote. It was narrated by al-Bukhari through the route of Yunus, and by Muslim through the route of Ma'mar. Muslim also recorded in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet, the encouragement to kill the gecko. All of this indicates its prohibition.

* *

The scholars also differed concerning the ibn awa (jackal/civet-like animal) and the ibn 'urs (weasel). Some scholars held that eating both is forbidden; this is the view of Imam Ahmad and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on them both. Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: Ahmad was asked about the ibn awa and the ibn 'urs, and he said: Everything that bites with its fangs from among the predators; and Abu Hanifa and his companions said the same. End of quote.

The position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is to differentiate between them. The ibn 'urs is lawful according to the Shafi'is without disagreement, because it has no strong fang, so it is like the lizard (dabb). The Shafi'is differed concerning the ibn awa.

Some of them said: its eating is lawful, because it does not strengthen itself with its fang, so it is like the rabbit.

The second view: it is not lawful, because it is considered repugnant and foul-smelling, and because it is of the kind of dogs. This was said by al-Nawawi. The apparent position of the school of Malik is that both are disliked.

As for the wabar and the yarbu': eating them is permissible according to Malik and his companions, and this is the school of al-Shafi'i and most of his companions, except that among them there is one opinion of prohibition regarding the wabar.

We have previously mentioned that 'Umar obligated a jafra (young female goat) for the yarbu', which indicates that it is game (sayd). The well-known position of Imam Ahmad also is the permissibility of eating the yarbu' and the wabar.

Among those who said the wabar is permissible: 'Ata', Tawus, Mujahid, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu Yusuf.

Among those who also said the yarbu' is permissible: 'Urwah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir, as the author of al-Mughni related from them.

The qadi among the Hanbalis said the wabar is forbidden. Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: This is also the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, except Abu Yusuf. He also said: Abu Hanifa said regarding the yarbu' too that it is forbidden, and this was narrated from Ahmad too, and from Ibn Sirin, al-Hakam and Hammad, because it resembles the mouse. al-Nawawi, in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab, related from the author of al-Bayan from Abu Hanifa the prohibition of the wabar, the yarbu', the dabb, the hedgehog and the ibn 'urs.

Among those who said the khuld and the darbub are permissible: Malik and his companions.

As for the hare (arnab): the verified position is that eating it is permissible, because it is established in the Two Sahihs from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ: "was presented with a leg of a hare and he accepted it," and in some narrations "and he ate from it." Ibn Qudamah said in al-Mughni: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas ate the hare; Abu Sa'id, 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Laith, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir permitted it, and we do not know of anyone who said it was forbidden except something narrated from 'Amr ibn al-'As. End of quote.

As for the dab (lizard/spiny-tailed lizard): the verified position also is the permissibility of eating it, because it is established in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet ﷺ said: «Eat, or feed others, for it is lawful», and said: «There is no harm in it, but it is not from my food», referring to the dab. And also established in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Khalid, may Allah be pleased with him: «that he ate a dab in the house of Maymunah, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was looking at it.» We have previously cited the statement of the author of al-Bayan from Abu Hanifa regarding the prohibition of the dab.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 145 (part 5 of 6):

The lizard (ḍabb) is also reported in *al-Mughni* as prohibited by Abu Hanifa and al-Thawri, and a prohibition on it is reported from Ali. We do not know of any basis for its prohibition except what Muslim reported in his *Sahih* from the hadith of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "was brought a lizard, and he refused to eat it," and said: "I do not know, perhaps it is of the earlier nations that were transformed (mukhtah)." Muslim also reported a similar hadith, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id. It seems that in this hadith he gave as the reason for abstaining from it the possibility of transformation, or that it bites, and so resembles the weasel (ibn 'urs). But this does not oppose the clear, sound evidence we have already presented for its permissibility. Some Arabs claimed that the lizard was among the nations that were transformed, as the words of the rajaz poet indicate:

"She said, and I was a clever man: 'By the life of Allah, this one is an Israelite (ʼisrā'īlīn)'."

This Arab woman swore that the lizard is an Israelite who was transformed.

* *

As for locusts: there is no disagreement among the scholars about the permissibility of eating them. It is established in the *Two Sahihs* from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa that he said: "We fought seven campaigns with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), eating locusts." End of quotation.

The carrion of locusts, without ritual slaughter (dhakah), is lawful according to the majority of scholars, based on the hadith: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us," and so on.
