Malik differed from the majority, requiring for its permissibility that it be ritually slaughtered (dhakah). In his view, the dhakah of locusts is whatever kills it with the intention of slaughter. This is the meaning of the words of Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki in his *Mukhtasar*: "Locust-like creatures require for it something that kills it, even if it is not hastened, such as cutting off a wing."

The Malikis argued for this position on the ground that the hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned above, "Two carrions have been made lawful for us," and so on, is not established, because its chains (turuq) are not free from weakness in the isnad (chain of narrators), or from being stopped at a companion (waqf). The default principle is the need for ritual slaughter, because of the generality of Allah's words: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

Ibn Kathir, in his commentary on Surat al-Ma'idah, said the following, and its text is: "Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam narrated to us from his father, from Ibn Umar, raised to the Prophet, who said: 'Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us. As for the two carrions: fish and locusts. As for the two bloods: the liver and the spleen.'" Likewise Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, and al-Bayhaqi narrated it from the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, and he is weak.

The hafiz al-Bayhaqi said: It was also narrated by Isma'il ibn Abi Idris from Usama, and from Abdullah, and from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ibn Umar, raised to the Prophet. I say: All three of them are weak, but some of them are better than others. It was narrated by Sulayman ibn Bilal, one of the reliable (athbat) transmitters, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ibn Umar, and some of them stopped it at Ibn Umar. The hafiz Abu Zur'a al-Razi said: This is more sound. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir. This is evidence for what the Malikis said. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The one who writes these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: However, the opponent may say that the narration stopped at Ibn Umar through the route of Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from him, is sound, and it has the status of a raised (marfu') report, because the saying of a companion, "It has been made lawful for us," or "It has been forbidden for us," has the status of a raised report. It is known that they do not make lawful for themselves, nor forbid for themselves, except that the Prophet (ﷺ) does so, as is established in the science of hadith. Al-Nawawi, in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, indicated that the sound narration stopped at Ibn Umar has the status of a raised report, as we mentioned, and this is clear. This is clear and unambiguous evidence for the permissibility of the carrion of locusts without ritual slaughter.

The Malikis said: The hadith is not established as raised to the Prophet. The carrion of locusts falls within the generality of His words: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾, the verse, and locusts require slaughter by something that kills them, such as cutting off their heads with the intention of slaughter, or by scalding them, or frying them.

Likewise there is also a narration from Imam Ahmad, which al-Nawawi transmitted from him in *Sharh Muslim* and *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

As for birds: all of their kinds are permissible to eat, except certain things about which scholars differ.

Among them is every bird with talons that strengthens itself with them and hunts, such as the falcon (saqr), the shahin, the baz, the eagle ('uqab), the peregrine (bashiq), and the like.

The majority of scholars are agreed on the prohibition of every bird with talons, as we have mentioned. Their evidence is the established prohibition on it in *Sahih Muslim* and elsewhere. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Abu Hanifa.

The position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is the permissibility of eating birds with talons, based on the generality of Allah's words: ﴿Say: I do not find...﴾ the verse. Also, no explicit text on the prohibition was established for him.

Among those who said as Malik said: al-Layth, al-Awza'i, and Yahya ibn Sa'id. Malik said: I have not seen anyone of the people of knowledge who disliked predatory birds. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik did not dislike eating any kind of bird: the vulture (rakhamah), the eagles, the hawks, the kite (hidaah), the crows, and all predatory birds and non-predatory birds, whether they eat carrion or do not.

There is no harm in eating the hoopoe (hudhhud) or the swallow (khuttaf). Ibn Rushd reported a dislike of eating the swallow, because its meat is scarce and it is forbidden for the one in whose house it nests. This is the end of what al-Mawwaq said in his commentary on Khalil's words in his *Mukhtasar*: "And a bird, even if it is a jallalah (an animal fed on filth)."

Among them are the kite (hidaah) and the spotted crow (al-ghurab al-abqa'), because they are among the *fawasiq* (vermin) that may be killed in the sacred and non-sacred areas. The permission to kill them is evidence of the prohibition of eating them. This is the position of the majority, in contrast to Malik and those who agreed with him, as we mentioned just above.

Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I am amazed at those who eat the crow, when the Prophet (ﷺ) has permitted its killing." The author of *al-Muhadhdhab*, after mentioning the prohibition on eating the spotted crow, said: The black large crow is also forbidden, because it is despised and eats carrion, so it is like the spotted one.

Regarding the *ghudaf* and the field crow (ghurab al-zar'), there are two opinions:
One: it is not lawful, because of the report.
The second: it is lawful, because it is considered good and pecks up grain, so it is like the pigeon and the chicken.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: Among them what eats carrion is forbidden, such as vultures, rakhams, the crow of separation (ghurab al-bayn), which is the largest of crows, and the spotted one. Urwa said: "Who would eat the crow, when the Prophet (ﷺ) named it a fasiq? By Allah, it is not among the good things." End of quotation.

The one who writes these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent and immediate meaning is that everything the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permitted to be killed without lawful ritual slaughter (dhakah shar'iyyah) is forbidden to eat, since if eating it were permissible he would not have permitted its destruction, as is clear.

Al-Nawawi said: The spotted crow is forbidden without dispute, because of the sound hadiths. For the large black one there are two routes: one, that it is forbidden; the other, that there are two opinions, the sounder of which is prohibition.

As for the field crow: there are two well-known opinions, the sounder of which is that it is lawful, and it is the *zaagh*, which is a small black bird, and it may have a reddish beak and legs. End of quotation, from it in summary, from *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*.

Among them: the sarad (a bird), the hoopoe, the swallow, and the bat (khuffash), which is the watawat.

The position of al-Shafi'i: the prohibition on eating the hoopoe and the swallow.

The author of *al-Muhadhdhab* said: Eating the hoopoe and the swallow is forbidden, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing them. Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: As for the hadith of the prohibition on killing the hoopoe, Ubayd Allah ibn Abdullah narrated it from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade killing four kinds of animals: the ant, the bee, the hoopoe, and the sarad. Abu Dawud narrated it with a sound isnad (chain) on the condition of al-Bukhari and Muslim; he mentioned it at the end of his book. Ibn Majah narrated it in the Book of Hunting with an isnad on the condition of al-Bukhari. As for the prohibition on killing the swallow, it is weak and mursal. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it with his isnad from Abu al-Huwayrith Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, who is one of the successors of the successors (taba' al-tabi'in) or of the successors (tabi'un), from the Prophet (ﷺ): "that he forbade killing the swallows." Then he said: Al-Bayhaqi said: This is interrupted (munqati'). He said: Hamza al-Nasibi narrated a hadith on this with a connected isnad, except that he was accused of forgery (wad'). End of quotation.

Among what al-Nawawi mentioned: you know that the sarad and the hoopoe are not lawful to eat in the school of al-Shafi'i, because the prohibition on killing them is established. Al-Nawawi also said: It is reported soundly from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, as a companion's saying (mawquf), that he said: "Do not kill frogs, for their croaking is glorification (tasbih). Do not kill the bat, for when Bayt al-Maqdis was destroyed it said: 'O Lord, give me power over the sea until I drown them.'" Al-Bayhaqi said: its isnad is sound.

The one who writes these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent reading in a matter like this, which is reported soundly from Abdullah ibn Amr, the prohibition on killing the bat and the frog, is that it has the status of a raised report, because there is no room for opinion in it. The knowledge of the frog's glorification and what the bat said cannot come by opinion. On this basis it is evidence for the prohibition on eating the bat and the frog.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: The swallow (khuttaf), the khushshaf, or the khuffash, which is the watawat, is forbidden. The poet said:

"Like the daylight, it increases the sight of creatures with light, and blinds the eyes of the bat."

Ahmad said: Who eats the khushshaf? He was asked about the swallow and said: I do not know. Al-Nakha'i said: Eating birds is lawful except the bat. These were forbidden only because they are considered repugnant, and the Arabs do not eat them. End of quotation from *al-Mughni*. The khushshaf is the khuffash. We have already mentioned from Malik and his companions the permissibility of eating all kinds of birds, and some of them excepted the watawat from this.

Regarding the parrot (babbagha) and the peacock (tawus), there are two opinions among the Shafi'is. Al-Baghawi and others said: The sounder of the two is prohibition.

Regarding the nightingale (andalib) and the hummingbird (humra), they also have two opinions. The sound one is their permissibility. Abu Asim al-Abbadi said: The "play-with-its-shadow" (mula'ib zillihi) is forbidden; it is a bird that swims in the air repeatedly, as if it swoops down upon a bird. Abu Asim also said: The owl (bum) is forbidden, like the vulture. He said: The *du'a'* (dhuwa'), with a dammed dad, an open waw, and an 'ayn, is forbidden according to the sounder of the two views. Al-Rafi'i said: This implies that the du'a' is other than the owl. He said: But in the *Sihah* of al-Jawhari, the du'a' is a bird of the night from the kind of the hamm (a bird of the owl family). Al-Mufaddal said: It is the male owl. Al-Rafi'i said: In that case, if there is a ruling on the du'a', it must be applied to the owl, since the male and female of a single kind do not differ. Al-Nawawi said this, then said: I say: the better-known view is that the du'a' is of the kind of the hamm, so there is no necessity that they share the ruling.

As for insects of birds, such as bees, wasps, flies, mosquitoes, and the like: eating them is forbidden according to al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and most scholars, because they are naturally repugnant. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And He forbids them the evil things﴾.

Among these is the jallalah, which is the animal that eats impurities. Its origin is the one that picks up *jillah*, with the jim having three vowels, which is dung. What the scholars mean by it is the one that eats impure substances, among birds and animals.

The well-known position of Imam Malik is the permissibility of eating the meat of the jallalah absolutely. As for its milk and urine, they are impure according to the well-known position in his school, as long as the impurity remains in its stomach. Its milk and urine become pure in his view if it abstains from eating impurities and is fed pure fodder for a period in which it is probable that nothing of the impure excretions remains in its stomach. Many scholars disliked the meat of the jallalah and its milk. Their proof is the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the milk of the jallalah." Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: The hadith of Ibn Abbas is sound. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i narrated it with sound chains. Al-Tirmidhi said: It is a hadith that is good and sound. End of quotation.

(p-543) Al-Nawawi said regarding the definition of the *jallalah* (an animal that feeds on filth): "The sound view, which the majority hold, is that quantity is not the criterion. The criterion is smell and stench. If the odour of impurity (*najasah*) is found in its sweat or elsewhere, it is a *jallalah*; otherwise, it is not. Eating the flesh of the *jallalah* and drinking its milk is disliked (*makruh*) according to the Shafi'is, and the sound view among them is that this is a disliking of *tanzih* (reprehensibility short of prohibition). It has also been said that it is a disliking of *tahrim* (prohibition)."

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: Ahmad said, "I dislike the flesh of the *jallalah* and its milk." Al-Qadi said in *al-Mujarrad*: "It is the animal that eats filth. If most of its fodder is impurity, its flesh and milk are forbidden." 

"As for its eggs, there are two reports. If most of its fodder is pure, its flesh and milk are not forbidden." The determination that the *jallalah* is one whose fodder is mostly impurity is something we have not heard from Ahmad, nor is it the apparent meaning of his words. However, it can be determined by what is abundant in its food, while what is little is excused. Al-Layth said: "They only disliked the *jallalah* that has no food except dung and the like." 

Ibn Abi Musa said: "Regarding the *jallalah* there are two reports. The first: it is forbidden. The second: it is disliked but not forbidden, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah disliked its flesh, and the practice is upon it until it is confined. Al-Hasan permitted its flesh and milk, because animals do not become impure by eating impurities, as evidenced by the fact that a drinker of wine is not judged to have his bodily parts made impure, and a disbeliever who eats pork and forbidden things does not have an impure outward appearance. Had he become impure, he would not have become pure through Islam or ritual bathing. And had the *jallalah* become impure, it would not have become pure through confinement." End of quotation.

The apparent ruling is that riding the *jallalah* is disliked. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Umar, and his son Abdullah. It was also reported from Ibn Umar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that riding the *jallalah* is disliked; al-Bayhaqi and others narrated it.

A young goat (*sakhlah*) raised on the milk of a bitch (*kalbah*) has, as far as is apparent, the same ruling as the *jallalah*, so what applies to it applies to it. And Allah knows best.

Among these matters are crops and fruits that were irrigated with impurities or fertilised with them. Most scholars hold that they are pure and that this does not render them impure. Among those who said so were Malik, al-Shafi'i, and their companions, in contrast to Imam Ahmad. Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: "Crops and fruits that were irrigated with impurities or fertilised with them are forbidden." Ibn Aqil said: "It is possible that this is disliked but not forbidden, and they are not judged impure, because the impurity transforms (*tastahil*) within them, and so becomes pure through transformation, like blood that transforms within the bodily parts of an animal into flesh and becomes milk. This is the view of most jurists, including Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas used to fertilise his land with *'arrah* (animal dung) and would say: "A basket of *'arrah* is a basket of wheat." *Al-'arrah* means human dung.

Our evidence is what is narrated from Ibn Abbas: "We used to rent out the lands of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we would stipulate on them that they not fertilise them with human dung." Also, because they (the crops) are nourished by impurities and their parts grow through them, and transformation does not purify. Accordingly, they become pure when irrigated with pure substances, just as the *jallalah* becomes pure when confined and fed pure things. End of quotation, from *al-Mughni* in its exact wording.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 148:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The ones who associated partners with Allah will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him"﴾, the verse. In this noble verse He mentions that they will say, "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated [partners]," and He mentions in another place that they actually said this, as in His saying in al-Nahl: ﴿And those who associated partners said: "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him"﴾, the verse [ \ 35 ], and His saying in al-Zukhruf: ﴿And they said: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾, the verse [ \ 20 ].

Their meaning is this: since Allah was able to prevent them from associating partners with Him, and did not prevent them, that is evidence of His approval of their polytheism. For this reason He refuted them here with His saying: ﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you could bring out for us? You follow nothing but conjecture"﴾ [al-An'am: 148], and He refuted them in al-Zukhruf with His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of this; they are only guessing﴾ [ \ 20 ], and He said in al-Zumar: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾, the verse [ \ 7 ].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The ones who associated partners with Allah will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated anything with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything"﴾, the verse.

This statement they made, considered in itself, is a true statement without doubt, because if Allah had willed, they would not have associated anything with Him, and would not have forbidden anything that He had not forbidden, such as the bahira and the sa'iba (kinds of animals they declared forbidden).

Allah has said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have associated [partners]﴾ [al-An'am: 107], and He said: ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [al-Sajda: 13], and He said: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 35]. If this statement that the disbelievers made is true, then what is the reason for Allah's refutation of them with His saying: ﴿Thus did those before them deny until they tasted Our punishment. Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you could bring out for us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you are only guessing"﴾ [al-An'am: 148]? A parallel to this very same problem occurs in surah "al-Zukhruf" in His saying: ﴿And they said: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of this; they are only guessing﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20].

The answer is that this statement the disbelievers made is a true statement, but it was intended for falsehood. So Allah's refutation of them falls upon their falsehood, which they intended by this true statement. Its clarification: their intention was that, since their disbelief and disobedience occurred by Allah's will, and that if He had willed He would have prevented them from it, then His not preventing them is evidence of His approval of their action. So Allah refuted them in this, clarifying that He does not approve of their disbelief, as He stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ (p-286) [al-Zumar: 7]. The disbelievers claimed that the universal will (al-irada al-kawniyya, the will of Allah as it occurs in creation) necessarily entails approval, and this is a false claim. Rather, Allah wills by His universal will what He does not approve, as is evidenced by His saying: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾ [al-Baqara: 7], together with His saying: ﴿And He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾. What truly entails approval is the legislative will (al-irada al-shar'iyya, the will of Allah as expressed in His commands), and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 151:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him"﴾

and the verse [continues]. The apparent meaning of His words "what your Lord has forbidden you" is that it is implicitly containing the meaning of "what your Lord has enjoined upon you," whether as an action or as an abstention, because abandoning an obligation and committing a forbidden act are both prohibited. So the meaning is: He has enjoined upon you ﴿that you not associate﴾ and that you show kindness to parents.

Allah, exalted is He, has made clear that this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you﴾ [al-An'am: 151 in the same sense], and so on.

* * *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty﴾, and so on. In this noble verse Allah, exalted is He, forbids killing children on account of poverty that has actually occurred. In Surat al-Isra' He forbids killing them out of fear of anticipated poverty that is feared, although it has not occurred at present, by His saying: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31]. The Prophet ﷺ clarified its meaning when 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, asked him: "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child out of fear that it will eat with you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit adultery﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and so on.

(p-545) Some scholars derived from this verse the prohibition of 'azl (coitus interruptus), since it is a hidden form of burying (infanticide). The hadith of Jabir: "We used to practise 'azl while the Revelation was descending" indicates its permissibility. However, a group of scholars said: it is not permitted with a free woman except with her permission, and it is permitted with a slave woman without her permission. Al-imlaq (الإملاق) means poverty. Some scholars said: al-imlaq means hunger.

An-Naqqash related it from Mu'arrij, and it was said: al-imlaq means spending (al-infaq); it is said: amlaqa malahu, meaning "he spent his wealth." He mentioned that 'Ali said to his wife: "Spend (amliqi) whatever you wish of your wealth."

This view is related from Mundhir ibn Sa'id; al-Qurtubi and others mentioned it. The correct view is the first.

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you"﴾, and the verse.

This verse indicates that what he recites to them is what their Lord has forbidden them, which gives the impression that the meaning of His words ﴿that you associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents﴾ [al-An'am: 151] is that kindness to parents and not associating are forbidden. The reality is otherwise, as is necessarily known.

Regarding this noble verse there is much discussion among the scholars, and many investigations and debates, which this brief treatment cannot encompass. Among them: that it is a relative clause (silah) as will come; and among them: that it has the meaning of "I will make clear to you, so that you do not associate."

Whoever obeys Satan while considering it lawful is a polytheist, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 121].

Among them: that the sentence is complete at His saying "your Lord has forbidden you," and that His saying "ʿalaykum allā tushrikū" is an expression (ism fi'l) whose complement relates to what follows, with its object being other than that. The closest of these views to us is what the Qur'an itself indicates, because the best way to interpret the Qur'an is by the Qur'an. That is: His saying, may He be exalted, "I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you" implicitly contains the meaning of "what your Lord has enjoined upon you," as abstention and as action. We say the Qur'an indicates this because Allah removed this difficulty and clarified His meaning by His saying: ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you, that you may understand﴾ [al-An'am: 151]. So the meaning is: He enjoined upon you that you not associate. A parallel in Arabic speech is the saying of the rajiz:

"He performed Hajj and enjoined on Sulayma, a slave, that she not see anyone and not speak to anyone."

After this, the closest views are two:

The first: the meaning is: "He makes it clear to you, so that you do not associate."

The second: that "an" in His saying "allā tushrikū" is explanatory of the prohibition. The objection to it, that His saying "and that this is My straight path" [al-An'am: 153] is conjoined to it, and that conjoining to it contradicts the explanation, is answered by the fact that the conjunction is not determined, since the preposition may be elided, so the meaning becomes: "and because this is My straight path, follow it," as one of them has held. However, the first view is the correct one, God willing, and according to it there is no difficulty in the verse at all.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 6, verse 152:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan except in the way that is best, until he reaches his maturity﴾, and the rest of the verse. A person without knowledge may mistakenly infer, from the implication by opposition (*mafhum al-mukhalafah*) of this noble verse, namely the implication of the limit (*mafhum al-ghayah*) in His saying ﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾ [al-An'am: 152], that once he reaches his maturity there is no barrier to approaching his property in ways other than the best. That is not what the verse intends. Rather, the limit of reaching maturity is meant to convey that if he reaches his maturity, his property is handed over to him provided that rectitude is perceived in him, as Allah explained by His saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them sound judgment, then hand over to them their property﴾ and the rest of the verse [an-Nisa': 6].

The correct view is that what is meant by *ashudd* (maturity) in this verse is puberty (*al-bulugh*), as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age, you perceive in them sound judgment﴾ and the rest of the verse.

Puberty is established by many signs: growth of hair, a boy's nocturnal emission, a girl's menstruation, and her becoming pregnant. Most scholars hold that the age of puberty is fifteen years. Some scholars said: when a person's stature reaches five spans (*ashbar*), he has reached puberty. This view is reported from Ali, and al-Farazdaq adopted it in his saying, lamenting Yazid ibn al-Muhallab: [Al-Kamil]

*He did not cease, since his hands tied his waistwrap, to rise until he attained the height of five spans,*
*drawing near the flapping [garments] of one flapping [garment] meeting,*
*in the shade of a dust-raised, dust-kicking, dust-stirring [place]*

As for *al-ashudd*, some scholars said: it is singular with no plural, like *al-anuk* (tin/lead alloy), which is lead. It was also said: its singular is *shadd*, like *fals* and *afls* (fils and fulus). This was stated by al-Qurtubi and others. And from Sibawayh it is reported that it is the plural of *shiddah* (strength), and its meaning is sound, because the Arabs say: "The boy reached his *shiddah*." However, the plural of *fi'lah* in the form *af'ul* is not well-attested, as al-Jawhari stated. As for *an'um*, it is not the plural of *ni'mah* (blessing); rather it is the plural of *ni'am*, from their saying *bi'sa* and *ni'ma* (bad/good). This was stated by al-Qurtubi, who also said: the origin of *al-ashudd* is from *shadd al-nahar*, meaning when the day rises. It is said: "I came to him at *shadd al-nahar*." Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Dabbi used to recite the verse of 'Antarah: [Al-Kamil]

*My acquaintance with him was at the rising of the day, as if he had dyed his chest and head with dark dye.*

Another poet said: [Al-Tawil]

*A woman-howdah (of a camel) circled around him at the rising of the day, long, with arms of a fine, tall, lean [form].*

The one who restricted this (the author) — may Allah pardon him — says: From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr: [Al-Basit]

*At the rising of the day, two forearms of a long-necked she-camel, slender, when she stood, were answered by weak, rounded [cries].*

So his saying "*shadd al-nahar*" means the time of its rising, and it is in apposition (*badal*) to "the day" in his preceding saying:

*A day when the wild ass keeps the mirage hot, as if its midday were pure sunlight.*

Thus *shadd al-nahar* is in apposition to his saying "a day," a partial apposition (*badal ba'd min kull*), just as his saying "a day" is in apposition to "when" (*idhā*) in his earlier saying: [Al-Basit]

*As if the return of her two forearms, when she sweats, and when she is wrapped in the thick, stacked clouds...*

This is because the time expressed by "when" (*idhā*) is precisely the same day mentioned in his saying "a day which keeps..." (the verse). A parallel in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿So when the great calamity comes, the day when man will remember what he strove for﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 34-35], and His saying: ﴿So when the deafening blast comes, the day a man will flee﴾ and the rest of the verse [Abasa: 33-34]. The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of Ka'b's verses here indicates the permissibility of overlapping apposition (*tadakhul al-badal*). His saying "two forearms of a long-necked she-camel" is the predicate of *ka'anna* in his saying "as if the return of her two forearms," (the verse).

Al-Suddi said: *al-ashudd* is thirty years. It was also said: forty years. It was also said: sixty years. It is not hidden that these opinions are far from the intended meaning of the verse, as we have explained, even though they are permissible linguistically, as Sukhaym ibn Wathil said: [Al-Wafir]

*A brother of fifty, my maturity gathered, and the varied dealings of affairs have tested me.*

* *

(p-546)

**Note**

Malik and his companions said: the sound judgment by which property is handed over to one who has reached marriageable age is the preservation of property and good management in disposing of it, even if he is a sinner and a heavy drinker. Likewise, a righteous and pious person who does not manage property well is not handed his property. Ibn 'Asim al-Maliki said in his *Tuhfah*: [Al-Rajaz]

*And a drinker of wine, when he becomes ... for what is under his control of his property, he will not be restricted.*
*And a righteous person who does not manage property well, if loss is feared, is restricted.*

Al-Shafi'i and those who agreed with him said: a sinful, disobedient person is not sound in judgment, because there is no greater folly than exposing oneself to the wrath and punishment of Allah by committing sins. And Allah knows best.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give full measure and weight in justice. We do not burden a soul except to its capacity﴾. In this noble verse, Allah commanded giving full measure and weight with justice, and mentioned that whoever fails to give it in full without intending to do so, there is no blame upon him for not intending it. He did not mention a punishment here for one who does so deliberately, but He threatened such a person with woe (*wayl*) in another place, and reproached him for not thinking that he will be resurrected on the Day of Judgment. That is in His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders, who, when they take a measure from people, take in full; but when they give by measure or weight to them, they cause loss. Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day, the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1-6].

In another place He mentioned that giving full measure and weight is better for its doer and better in outcome, in His saying: ﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true balance. That is better and more favorable in outcome﴾ [al-Isra': 35].

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative﴾. In this noble verse, Allah commanded justice in speech, even if it is against a close relative. In another place He explicitly commanded this even if it is against oneself or one's parents, in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and close relatives﴾ and the rest of the verse [an-Nisa': 135].

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah﴾ and the rest of the verse. In this noble verse, Allah commanded fulfilling the covenant of Allah. In another place He explicitly stated that the covenant of Allah will be questioned about on the Day of Judgment, in His saying: (p-548) ﴿And fulfill the covenant, for the covenant will be questioned about﴾ [al-Isra': 34], meaning: about it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 157:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or you should say, "If the Book had been revealed to us, we would surely have been better guided than they."﴾ etc. In this noble verse, He mentions that one of the purposes of revealing the Great Qur'an is to cut off the excuse of the disbelievers of Makkah, so that they do not say: "If a Book had been revealed to us, we would have acted upon it, and we would have been better guided than the Jews and the Christians, who did not act upon their books." In another place He declared that they swore to this, and that when it was revealed to them, its revelation only increased them in aversion and distance from the truth, because of their arrogance and their evil scheming. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be better guided than any of the nations.﴾ ﴿But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion,﴾ ﴿in arrogance in the land and evil scheming. And evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its own people.﴾ [Fatir: 42].

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah and turns away from them?﴾ etc.

Some scholars said: the verb in this verse, meaning "ṣadafa" (صدف, to turn away), is intransitive, and its meaning is "he turned away from them." This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

As-Suddi said: "ṣadafa" (صدف) in this verse is transitive to an object, and the object is omitted; the meaning is that he diverted others from following the signs of Allah. The Qur'an supports the view of as-Suddi, because the turning away of this person, than whom no one is more unjust, from the signs of Allah, is stated in His saying: ﴿So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 157]. For there is no turning away greater than denial. This shows that the intended meaning of His saying, "and turns away from them," is that he diverted others from them, so he combines error with misguiding others.

On the first view, the meaning of "ṣadafa" (صدف) is dispensed with by His saying "denies" (kadhdhaba, كذب). The parallel of the verse according to the view that the Qur'an supports, which is the view of as-Suddi, is His saying: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾, and His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of Allah, We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾ [an-Nahl: 88].

The statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Mujahid may be interpreted as follows: the intended meaning of his denial and turning away is that his heart did not believe in them, and his limbs did not act upon them. A parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed.﴾ ﴿But he denied and turned away﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31-32], and similar verses that indicate the disbeliever's containing denial in his heart and abandonment of action with his limbs. Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir, after pointing to this: "But the statement of as-Suddi is stronger and more evident, and Allah knows best." End quote.

The use of "ṣadafa" (صدف) in the sense of "turned away" is common in the speech of the Arabs. Among it is the saying of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith:

Meter: al-Tawil

I marvel at Allah's judgment concerning us, when His outright turning away from every revealed truth has become apparent to Him.

It is narrated that Ibn 'Abbas recited the verse of Abu Sufyan for this meaning. Also among it is the saying of Ibn ar-Riqa':

Meter: al-Basit

When they mention a narration, they say the best of it, and they are "ṣadaf" (صدف) from every evil that is to be avoided.

That is: they are turning away.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or that your Lord should come?﴾ In this noble verse, He mentioned the coming of Allah, glory be to Him, and His angels on the Day of Resurrection. He mentioned this in another place and added that the angels will come in rows, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angel, rank upon rank.﴾ [al-Fajr: 22] He mentioned it in yet another place and added that He, glory be to Him and exalted, comes in canopies of clouds, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. Such is the case with the attributes (sifat) of Allah, may He be exalted, which He ascribed to Himself: they are passed on as they came, one believes in them, holds that they are true, and holds that He is not like any of the attributes of the created beings. Glory be to Him who encompasses everything in knowledge: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, but they do not encompass Him in knowledge.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 110]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 6, verse 162:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, indeed my prayer and my sacrifice﴾ — the verse.

Some scholars said: What is meant by nusuk (sacrifice, act of worship) here is slaughtering (al-nahr), because the disbelievers used to draw near to their idols by an act of worship that is among the greatest of acts of worship: slaughtering. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet to say that his prayer and his slaughtering are both sincerely for Allah, exalted is He. The saying of Allah, exalted is He, supports this: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾ [al-Kawthar: 2]. Other scholars said: nusuk includes all acts of worship, and slaughtering is included within it. Others among them said: what is meant by His saying, "and sacrifice," is placing the right hand upon the left under the chest during prayer. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.
